A primary component of this enhancement involves a completely new inner tracking system, designed as a high-granularity silicon structure capable of operating in an environment with substantially higher pileup conditions. This upgraded system features a shorter radius than current instruments, begins at just 2.5 cm from the interaction point, and incorporates a higher number of layers to ensure robust photon reconstruction even amidst higher pileup. Furthermore, the new inner tracker will utilize 50% more silicon sensor area than today's innermost segments. Despite the higher radiation levels anticipated at the beginning of High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) Run 3 and beyond, the design employs 100% more bonding area per chip, resulting in approximately 2.5 times the bonding area per square centimeter of sensor compared to modern LHC ATLAS readout technologies. To validate the feasibility of this novel design, a proof-of-principle (PoP) prototype was constructed. This prototype utilizes modern 80 MHz, 1.5 Gb/s, 8T/8D SERDES (Series-Parallel) I/Os, a 28 nm CMOS process, and fully differential circuitry. Testing of the PoP prototype in an HL-LHC-representative, high-pileup environment confirmed its successful reconstruction of photons as close as 2.5 cm from the interaction point, verifying the viability of this readout architecture for full-scale production. Additionally, the PoP platform demonstrated performance, power, and area efficiency gains of up to 60% to 100% relative to existing commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) alternatives. Beyond its potential for the full HL-LHC scale-up, this PoP design marks a significant milestone in exploring advanced application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) architectures for future particle physics experiments.

Extending DNR to handle articulated objects via skinned meshes is a logical step that could expand its applicability; however, this requires the neural shading stage to manage mesh deformations that may be imperfectly captured, alongside alignment errors and dynamic movements, all of which can disrupt the DNR pipeline. To address these challenges for virtual human avatars, we introduce Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a new framework built upon DNR. Our results demonstrate that ANR outperforms both the original DNR and methods specifically designed for avatar creation and animation. Two user studies reveal a distinct preference for our avatar model, while quantitative metrics confirm state-of-the-art performance. In terms of perception, ANR offers superior temporal stability, detail, and plausibility, and it supports multiple poses simultaneously. Quantitatively, ANR requires roughly 10× less memory, 200× fewer parameters, and 1000× fewer frames per second during optimization compared to avatar-specific approaches, with a 50× smaller model size. Additionally, ANR supports up to 1000 simultaneous subjects, a capability unattainable by prior avatar methods. Our code and datasets are publicly available.

We aim to train a neural network to render a 3D object from any viewpoint using only unstructured 2D image inputs. Unlike approaches that rely on initial mesh or voxel representations, our method utilizes only collections of unstructured 2D images. Each image provides pixel-level correspondence, allowing us to encode both appearance and geometry within neural networks. By formulating the problem as an energy minimization task, we can synthesize views of the target object from these images alone. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing techniques, such as Neural Poisson and DNR, both subjectively and objectively. Furthermore, our approach is highly versatile, successfully processing images of a real human, a ferret, and a 1950s car.

Processing dense 3D point clouds is essential for numerous real-world applications, yet current learning-based methods struggle with computational inefficiency, memory constraints, and a lack of generality. To overcome these hurdles, we propose Point Eraser Networks (PEN), which process arbitrarily large and dense 3D point clouds with the simplicity, memory effectiveness, and flexibility of point-based volumetric reasoning. how changes in local structure influence functional properties, a challenge best addressed through advanced experimental and computational methods. In this study, we compare two techniques for deriving local structural parameters from scattering data: the conventional Fourier transform method and the Maximum Entropy Method (MEM). Using the crystal GaInAs as a case example, we demonstrate that MEM effectively yields realistic local structural information that aligns closely with initial model assumptions and complementary computational predictions. However, we also identify limitations, most notably the inability of MEM to accurately resolve broad multi-atom correlations at large distances. We explicitly calculate these multi-atom correlations at GaInAs interfaces, confirming their width and shape as predicted by computational studies. Furthermore, we show how combining MEM with other complementary approaches enables the accurate determination of both short- and long-range local structural characteristics. Finally, we discuss how this synergy can enhance our understanding of the relationship between the atomic structure and physical properties of disordered materials. As a practical note, we explicitly present the GaInAs scattering functions, which can serve as a reference for future investigations into similar III-V disordered alloys. Additionally, we provide an appendix detailing the unique features and constraints of MEM, serving as a guide for correctly applying the method to specific problems.

Atomic hydrogen serves as a fundamental building block for numerous advanced materials, yet it often exhibits adverse effects on the electronic and structural stability of two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) stacks. By combining first-principles calculations with maximum entropy method (MEM) analysis of electron density, we show that adsorbing a single H atom on black phosphorus (BP) causes the P$_4$ rings to collapse into a linear chain, resulting in an unstable, metallic, and highly reactive $\gamma$-BP phase. In contrast, adding two H atoms to opposite sides of an exfoliated BP sheet creates a stable, insulating, and robust 2D vdW stack known as H$_2$-BP. The electron density distribution of this new material reveals a bilayer structure with a sandwich-like arrangement of atomic layers, where the interlayer spacing closely matches the thickness of an exfoliated BP sheet. This finding confirms that the structural robustness of H$_2$-BP arises from the synergistic stabilization of bp-biphenylene fragments by atomic hydrogen, effectively suppressing the Peierls distortion typically observed in bare BP sheets. The objective is to estimate $E_G(\eta(\theta)) \equiv \eta_G$ using independent observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$, given that $Y_i \sim f(y|\theta_i)$ and $\theta_i \sim G$ are independent and identically distributed. This work investigates Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) for this scenario, outlining their fundamental properties and representations. Specifically, we propose a novel viewpoint on the weak convergence result by Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956), extending its implications to a setting where $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n$ are treated as fixed parameters. Furthermore, we connect the problem of estimating $\eta_G$ to nonparametric empirical Bayes estimation under squared loss. The GMLE is demonstrated to yield a substantial reduction in risk compared to the naive estimator $\bar\eta_n \equiv \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\eta(\theta_i)$. Additionally, we address the minimax risk for the estimator of $\eta_G$ and establish a connection to Tsiatis's work (1983). The findings are illustrated through examples of Poisson and normal means and distributions.

Independent observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ follow distributions from a parametric model $f(y|\theta)$, $\theta \in \Omega$, where each parameter $\theta_i$ is a draw from an unknown distribution $G$, and $\Omega$ is a metric space. We examine the estimator for $E[G(\cdot)](\Omega)$ that minimizes the risk under a specific loss function $L(G,\cdot)$. Specifically, we explore the link between this estimation task and empirical Bayes methods, extending the framework of Tsiatis (1983). Under the assumption that the data $\{Y_i, i=1, \dots, n\}$ are i.i.d., the estimator is shown to admit a representation via the GMLE introduced by Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) and Wolfe (1968). Additionally, we analyze an extension of the risk function where the mixing distribution $G$ is not necessarily determined by $n$ data points, even when $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n$ are fixed.

AL identifies which subset of educational activities yields the highest knowledge gain per learning resource, typically leveraging transfer learning (TL) and data from the student's history. However, in keyAL, which AL systems for learning (ASALs) must operate on data dissimilar to the student's training sets, a data domain shift challenge arises. While TL helps bridge some of this gap, it can also introduce negative transfer, where similarities between domains hinder performance in the target domain. To address this, we propose a novel ensemble (EE) strategy that combines ASALs trained on multiple source domains with a primary system using an adaptive weight selection mechanism. Our results indicate that EE outperforms individual ASALs and other ensemble methods, even when those primary systems suffer from severe domain shifts. Additionally, we show that incorporating adaptive weight selection into ASALs significantly mitigates the risks of negative transfer and enhances overall performance. A key contribution of this study is the demonstration that ASALs, despite facing data domain shifts, can effectively improve student outcomes by utilizing student historical data. We further evaluate EE and its variants against baseline ASALs and existing ensemble methods (AL) across two real-world datasets. The findings reveal that EE achieves better or comparable performance to other ensembles under AL conditions but surpasses them significantly when accounting for domain shifts, with an average improvement of 9.4% over the best-performing AL system. Finally, we provide interpretations of the model's internal structure to validate these insights.

AL systems are designed to select a subset of learning activities that maximize a student's knowledge acquisition relative to the time invested. Our study focuses on two primary objectives: (1) developing a student model capable of predicting a student's potential knowledge gain, and (2) applying optimization techniques to identify the activity subset that maximizes this gain. To handle data domain shifts, we employ a semi-supervised deep neural network. We evaluate our approach on two real-world datasets, validating its effectiveness in selecting activities that enhance AL outcomes despite domain disparities.

In AL, the goal is to determine the set of activities that best promotes a student's knowledge, considering both the potential gain and the associated time cost. We introduce a novel ASAL that utilizes a semi-supervised deep neural network to predict a student's potential knowledge gain across target domains. SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed to identify and rectify errors in SMT solver results. This process requires the format to explicitly list the assumptions and guarantees (invariants) associated with each node. However, the original standard library definition lacked support for these invariants. The veriT extension to this library is now presented, illustrating how the format can be defined using standard invariants. Furthermore, the node types and operations of the format are outlined, followed by an explanation of how to locate proofs of specific formulas and perform node substitution within the format. Additionally, a mapping between the original and extended node types is provided to facilitate the identification of errors in veriT proofs when a given assertion is incorrect. Notably, the first and last nodes of the proof chain share identical invariant profiles, which, although offering limited space for distinct first-node proofs, enables the incorporation of more complex proofs at the head of the chain. A demonstration of this capability is now provided. The presentation concludes with a note on how veriT was selected for the DARPA First-Order Proof Format (FO^2) challenge a few years ago. veriT was chosen specifically because it utilized a proof format that did not support invariants, thereby necessitating an extension to meet the challenge's requirements. The FO^2 format, as defined a couple of years prior, is now briefly reviewed. Finally, an extension to veriT is discussed that aligns it more closely with the specifications of the FO^2 format. veriT, /, and FO^2 are indexed terms.

We introduce a format designed for producing human-readable proofs using the TPTP system. In this scheme, every logic symbol functions as a variable; thus, an atomic formula like $f(x_1, x_2)$ is treated as a labeled node (specifically, one with the 'f' label) whose arguments are $x_1$ and $x_2$. Consequently, compound formulas are viewed as sequences of such nodes. Consequently, any formula can be interpreted as a labeled graph, where nodes and edges are clearly defined. Complementary to our prior presentation on how veriT supports the generation of this format, we now examine how other proof formats can be translated into it.

While theoretically sound, the standard SFTL algorithm risks failing during practical, multi-round cross-device federated learning because of two main issues: (1) the necessity of a SFTL label distribution that is identically or nearly so across devices, and (2) the requirement for theoretical guarantees of convergence to a stationary point. This paper investigates these obstacles from a practical perspective and proposes two corresponding remedies. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed similarity threshold for theoretical convergence and develop an approach to adaptively update this threshold online. Furthermore, we propose two methods to adaptively update global model weights, allowing the algorithm to function effectively even when the shared label distribution is not modally similar, thereby enhancing the robustness and robustness of SFTL. Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach. In summary, our contributions address the limitations of existing theoretical analyses by providing practical guidance for label distribution alignment, improving both robustness and reliability in multi-round federated learning. The effectiveness of the proposed simultaneous update and adaptive threshold strategies is validated both theoretically and empirically. These theoretical findings are also applicable to decentralized learning and other multi-task learning scenarios that share a similar framework. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyuan2000/SFTL_revised.

Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, transferring from English (with 10x more data) to Czech-based WER decreased from 12.9% to 10.9%, while leveraging the intermediate alphabet further reduced the WER to 9.8%. Additionally, using the intermediate alphabet alone yielded a substantial 5% relative decrease in WER compared to processing Czech text directly. These findings indicate strong potential for increasing ASR accessibility and lowering the barrier to entry, particularly when dealing with low-resource languages. The source code and models are available here: https://github.com/CTA-IR/CTA_IRA_2021.

This paper introduces a novel, diverse social network dataset named "Twitch Gamers," which features multiple potential target attributes. Our analysis of the network structure and subsequent node classification experiments demonstrate that the Twitch Gamers dataset is well-suited for evaluating the predictive capabilities of innovative proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embedding methods. The dataset is publicly accessible at https://doi.org/10.15480/1129338_610.

Although network science has developed numerous methods to identify nodes with distinct functional roles within complex networks, these significant entities often remain unnoticed by scientists and the public. While previous studies have attempted to find nodes with unique structural roles using local network features as their sole indicator, this research presents a novel method for identifying such nodes in complex networks.

Node classification involves assigning labels to network nodes based on their features, a task with wide-ranging applications in science and industry, including spam detection, disease gene identification, and community discovery. Traditional algorithms rely heavily on explicit node features, but these are often difficult or impossible to obtain for large-scale networks. Consequently, this paper introduces a network-based learning algorithm that functions effectively even when node features are unavailable. We assessed the algorithm's performance on six real-world datasets, confirming that node labels can be accurately predicted based on node neighborhood structures despite the absence of feature information.

Precise labeling of individual nodes within a network is essential for various tasks, yet acquiring node features is often impractical, especially in large-scale networks. This work aims to assign labels to individual nodes using solely network information, even when feature data is unobtainable. Although algorithmically sound, this approach remains unproven in large-scale networks with missing features. This paper reports on large-scale experiments where nodes were successfully labeled on networks featuring missing features, validating the algorithm's efficacy in this context.

Although scientific inquiry has identified that social network nodes can be categorized into different roles, existing classification algorithms struggle to accurately predict node labels when feature information is unavailable. This study examines whether the performance of scientific classification algorithms can be enhanced by incorporating the role information of nodes. The findings indicate that integrating role data can improve the accuracy of scientific classification, a benefit that is particularly relevant given the rarity of feature information in many networks.

Furthermore, the $f_X(1500)$ displays an excited state in its transverse mass distribution at around 2.2 GeV$^2$, which aligns closely with the predicted $K^2$ value for the 2P orbital of (anti)charm quarks. In contrast, the $f_2(1525)$ lacks such an excitation in its transverse mass spectrum, consistent with its 1P orbital assignment. Finally, the measured width of the $f_X(1500)$ is compatible with expectations derived from its constituent quark composition.

We demonstrate that the Hawking radiation rate for black holes sensitive to this dark dimension is reduced by a factor proportional to $(10^{-5}/R)^2$, where $R$ is measured in micrometers. Consequently, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately $10^{11}$ grams would fail to completely evaporate by the present day, leaving a remnant with a mass of roughly $10^{11}$ grams. This implies an upper limit on the abundance of such primordial black holes, which, when combined with a minimally supermassive lower bound, results in an order of magnitude tighter constraint on the density of dark matter that can be accounted for by these objects. Furthermore, if primordial black holes are confirmed to constitute any portion of the dark matter, it would suggest an inverse relationship between an object's mass and its formation probability, a hallmark of theories involving one or more dark dimensions. We establish that a broad class of models featuring a single dark dimension satisfies this requisite mass-probability trade-off. Additionally, we argue that within a specific framework where the dark dimension arises from a higher-categorical symmetry, the lower mass bound is actually Refined Swampland bounds, setting a limit of approximately $10^{10}$ grams. We also examine the impact of gravitational binding energy on both the evaporation and mass limits, finding that if such energy contributes to dark matter, it would further tighten the constraint to about $10^{9}$ grams. Finally, we explore the hypothesis that an entire asteroid belt could have been ejected from a star system due to the formation of a primordial black hole, concluding that if dark matter is represented by such asteroid-like structures, their mass could not be less than $10^{23}$ grams. If primordial black holes account for any fraction of dark matter, it necessitates an upward revision of any lower mass bound for asteroid-like matter derived from the stability of main-belt asteroids.

Designed to address poor force measurements in SEAs resulting from elastic transmission nonlinearities, sensor noise, and deformation measurement errors, the paper first examines the limitations of traditional SEA force sensing methods and analyzes their stochastic properties, laying the groundwork for accurate force control via TFOB. Notably, a tuning parameter is derived from holistic closed-loop frequency domain analyses, offering a framework to achieve optimal performance in force-controlled SEA systems. The efficacy of the proposed algorithm is validated through experiments on a physical SEA hardware platform. Results demonstrate that the combined algorithm and tuning parameter strategy significantly enhance performance, with the TFOB achieving a high accuracy of 98.13% in force measurement. This approach is anticipated to yield promising outcomes for future research in SEA force control.

This study introduces a force control scheme for cable-driven robots (CDRs) featuring series elastic actuators (SEAs), utilizing an elastic vibration-based friction compensation method (EVM-FC). Unlike conventional SEA control systems that rely on direct measurement of elastic forces, this system uses link acceleration to infer elastic force, a strategy termed external force-based friction compensation control (EFB-FC). The EVM-FC achieves superior force control performance by integrating a sliding mode control algorithm, a resonance suppression term, and a resonance enhancement term.

I. INTRODUCTION

Automating marine tasks through robot fleets offers substantial advantages for both research and industrial applications. However, these systems face numerous challenges, with accurate target localization being a primary concern. While underwater robots (AUVs) are well-suited for long-duration missions in deep sea settings, they rely on camera data to identify and track marine targets. Despite progress in vision-based autonomic targeting, AUVs continue to struggle with data efficiency and prediction accuracy when gathering sonar imagery.

To address these issues, this paper offers practical solutions by: 1) enhancing data efficiency through the application of Temporal Difference (TD) learning, 2) improving prediction quality, and 3) increasing robustness against environmental variability.

Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the competition, including insights gained from the leaderboards and findings derived from an examination of top-performing public submissions. Our analysis reveals that public contributions primarily fall into three categories: 1) modifications to the standard ResNet backbone, such as altering channel dimensions, applying channel attention mechanisms, or incorporating feature pyramid learning; 2) the application of various self-supervised contrastive learning approaches, including but not limited to MoCo, Barlow Twins, and ASL; and 3) the implementation of heavy-weighted segmentation and classification models, such as Swin-TR, TransUNet, and others. General Policy Improvement is a foundational theory underlying many contemporary deep reinforcement learning algorithms. This paper introduces Two Network General Policy Improvement (TNGPI), which employs a dual-network structure to simultaneously estimate the score function and the critic. We demonstrate that the TNGPI framework avoids several vulnerabilities inherent in its single-network counterpart. Both theoretical analysis and empirical experiments are provided to validate the advantages of the proposed method.

Although extensive research has been conducted on theoretical assurances for policy search, these efforts often rely on complex and abstract frameworks that obscure the design of practical algorithms. The General Policy Improvement (GPI) principle, which iteratively performs local policy improvements via sufficient policy evaluations, offers a clear design blueprint for modern deep reinforcement learning. We present the Deep GPI algorithm, a specific implementation of this principle, and illustrate how various existing deep learning methods can be viewed as specialized instances of Deep GPI. Based on this perspective, we derive the convergence rate for a Markov Decision Process, offering the first practical and straightforward guarantee for deep reinforcement learning. This establishes a unifying framework for the field and highlights the significance of sufficient policy evaluation. Our findings provide a rational basis for constructing efficient algorithms, such as using a critic network to estimate the critic in TRPO, and reveal the core relationships among diverse methods like SAC, TD3, and TDC.

# Introduction

The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) has generated vast quantities of sensitive data from a diverse array of sources. Consequently, there is an urgent requirement for frameworks capable of securing data directly at the source, ideally enabling users to perform computations on data without it needing to leave their devices. Cloud computing has emerged as a primary solution, offering on-demand access to scalable computing resources and services. However, despite its many advantages, cloud computing introduces significant security challenges and vulnerabilities. Although cloud providers provide robust access controls, the scale of data they process, combined with the inherent complexity of cloud environments, creates numerous potential attack vectors. One of the most significant vulnerabilities is the side-channel leakage, where system resources—such as execution time, power consumption, memory access patterns, and network traffic—are exposed.

In high-throughput settings, where multiple individuals undergo similar procedures over time (e.g., online health or social platforms), resource overlaps make these systems particularly susceptible to inference attacks. Attackers can deduce sensitive information about individual identities and characteristics by analyzing how system resources are consumed during data processing.

# Introduction
Understanding protoplanetary disk evolution requires modeling two distinct processes: viscous mass redistribution and the formation of companion bodies like planets. Viscosity drives mass migration inward, causing accretion onto the central star, a process well-described by standard viscous disk models. Consequently, hydrodynamic simulations are essential for investigating how these additional ingredients influence disk evolution and the formation of embedded bodies.

In the past few decades, the income gap in the United States has widened markedly, prompting debates on its causes and implications. While some attribute this rise to technological advancement, market competition, and globalisation, others argue that a societal focus on inequality has itself driven further divergence. To evaluate these hypotheses, researchers must understand how people form beliefs about the origins of economic success and how these beliefs correlate with actual outcomes. This paper presents an experimental method for uncovering a specific mechanism: the "myth of meritocracy."

The myth of meritocracy posits that individuals hold stronger beliefs in a meritocratic system when they can observe a direct link between luck and outcomes. In such scenarios, even those who experienced bad luck view the system as favoring merit, assuming that others who faced similar fortune would have succeeded similarly. Conversely, in settings where luck does not directly affect outcomes, individuals who thrive are perceived as talented, leading to a belief that the system rewards talent. Since higher inequality is often associated with greater reliance on market forces where luck matters, this myth offers an explanation for why increased inequality does not necessarily diminish, and may even foster, attitudes toward redistribution.

Consequently, if the atoms within a fully thermal ensemble exhibit specific fluctuations, there exists a corresponding non-thermal atomic system with complementary fluctuation properties that, when integrated, yield zero net fluctuations. The construction of a fully thermal atomic ensemble is practically achievable at sufficiently high temperatures and/or short observation times relative to the inter-atomic interaction timescale. Online multi-agent reinforcement learning trains agents within a live environment, relying on continuously gathered transition data. Unlike clean datasets, this data often includes irrelevant actions not present in the agent's current action space, necessitating action space alignment before update. We propose a general offline multi-agent reinforcement learning framework capable of handling both consistent and inconsistent action spaces, subsuming behaviors like BC and SP as special cases. By leveraging agent interaction graphs and a learned interaction function, our method unifies these existing approaches and ensures consistency during inference. This event triggered three decades of theoretical development culminating in the Bell Theorem. In this work, we employ an analogous approach to reveal how the pre-measurement state of one system evolves nonlocally over time. High Energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (HECAM) is to locate and track transients in the gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical bands, as well as the solar system, with an accuracy of a few arcseconds using real-time astrometry at the millisecond level. This goal will support the third-generation Gravitational Wave detector network, expected to go online around 2030, which features improved sensitivity, broader frequency coverage, higher signal-to-noise ratios, and better directional reconstruction. To achieve this, HECAM must rapidly identify, characterize, and localize gravitational wave (GW) signals and precursors (such as neutron star crust fractures) to enable the deployment of GW-derived trigger lists for rapid follow-up by other observatories. Furthermore, by studying known and newly discovered astrophysical transients, HECAM aims to refine the characterization of GW sources, enhance their localization, and support population studies. The telescope array will consist of 2,048 fully independent, wide-field, CMOS-based optical cameras, each with a 0.5-degree field of view and capable of X-ray to optical sensitivity. Complementary to this array, a few dozen highly sensitive, fully steerable, wide-field, CMOS-based imaging cameras will provide better localization and characterize the system's wide-field light curves. Designed for the multi-messenger astronomy era, HECAM is proposed to the National Science Foundation's Decadal Survey as a Ground-Based Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) add-on, leveraging the LSST's rapid re-pointing capability and deep legacy survey. HECAM requires a dedicated control, monitoring, and data acquisition building housing approximately 2,048 camera controllers, a few hundred kilowatts of electric power, and roughly 100 square kilometers of data cabling. This white paper outlines the scientific case for HECAM, reviews its design and technical specifications, and provides a cost estimate, demonstrating that the system is both feasible and cost-effective. As the most sensitive and accurate all-sky monitor for transients, HECAM would significantly advance the study of gamma-ray bursts, fast radio bursts, TDEs, kilonovae, supernovae, neutron star and black hole binaries, and other fast-evolving phenomena. This document serves as a summary of the detailed technical design report available at https://github.com/LSST-DESC/HECAM-WP.

Over the last half-century, the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has developed rapidly, enabling machines to emulate human abilities and, more recently, the third generation of deep learning-based intelligent systems has achieved significant milestones. The deep learning framework, characterized by neural networks (NNs) with multiple layers, has yielded remarkable outcomes in various domains, most notably within Natural Language Processing (NLP). In NLP, deep learning has been extensively applied to enhance part-of-speech tagging, sentence parsing, and word alignment, with the latter proving particularly pivotal for Cross-Linguistic Knowledge Transfer (CLKT). CLKT aims to leverage linguistic knowledge from resource-rich languages to improve Natural Language Understanding (NLU) in resource-scarce languages by learning language-agnostic representations that capture language-specific features.

This paper presents an end-to-end framework for CLKT, integrating language-agnostic representation learning with sequence labeling. The proposed system, named Knowledge Transfer Learning for NLU (KTL), employs a NN architecture comprising a stacked bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) layer followed by a series of fully connected (FC) layers. These components collectively learn language-agnostic representations that encode both general and language-specific features, facilitating effective knowledge transfer from rich to poor languages.

Experimental results across part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing tasks demonstrate the system's efficacy, showing substantial improvements in languages with abundant resources transferred to those with scarce data. Furthermore, system evaluations at the Shared Task on Universal Dependencies (UD) 2019 have validated the system's competitiveness within the broader AI community.

The system and this report were developed under the guidance of Prof. Dr. Rainer Downey, a senior researcher at the University of Hamburg, during the 2019 Shared Task on Universal Dependencies. Additionally, the system participated in the UD 2020 shared task, and this report aligns with the report generated at that event.

In this architecture, the base station (BS) leverages its aperture to transmit via an optical direct link directly to the destination or through an optical relay, while simultaneously utilizing a radio frequency (RF) multi-element antenna system to transmit data via an indirect multi-hop RF link to the destination. To ensure Q-factor compliance for optical multi-hop free-space optical (FSO) relay systems, this design offers a viable alternative when direct optical paths fail due to atmospheric turbulence. Specifically, the BS establishes an indirect optical link to the destination through an intermediate optical relay known as an FSO relay, which operates at a different spectrum than the RF link. Suitable precoding weights are derived based on the channel conditions of both transmitting systems to optimize end-to-end throughput. Assuming independent Rayleigh fading for RF links and Kolmogorov turbulence for optical links, the study derives the end-to-end throughputs, outage probabilities, and secrecy outage probabilities (SOP) for all possible transmission paths in closed forms. Additionally, in a scenario where an eavesdropper intercepts signals from both diverse-spectrum links, the SOP is also calculated in a closed form. Numerical simulations are presented to examine the impacts of the number of antenna elements, direct optical link strength, atmospheric conditions, and eavesdropper locations on the system's secrecy performance. The results indicate that the dual-spectrum PLS system consistently outperforms single-spectrum PLS systems, even in the presence of an eavesdropper, due to the use of different communication spectra. Furthermore, introducing an eavesdropper in an indirect relay link significantly enhances the SOP compared to a direct link, a finding that is further explored when an eavesdropper is present in an entire dual-spectrum system. Finally, this work is extended to a full-duplex direct optical link, and the effects of an eavesdropper and atmospheric conditions on the SOP are discussed. This research confirms the high potential of the proposed dual-spectrum diverse-transmit system for effective and secure data transmission. This is followed by the examination of an optical multi-hop relay system with an eavesdropper on an indirect link featuring time-reversal self-interference. Consequently, the findings regarding an indirect optical relay with an eavesdropper are compared against a direct optical relay with an eavesdropper to determine the maximum acceptable average cross-talk for maintaining a satisfactory SOP.

This study examines the impact of shifting travel times and volumes on the feasibility of achieving a specific throughput target at one such intersection. We introduce a novel macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) that integrates a time-dependent arrival function with a MFD derived from a cell transmission model. This framework enables the prediction of departing volumes based on evolving arriving and departing time distributions, accounting for queues on both approaches, the mainstreet upstream of the approach, and stored vehicles. The mainstreet MFD serves as the foundation for an integrated traffic simulation and control methodology, capable of managing departing volumes even when mainstreet congestion influences street conditions. Although situated at a microscopic level, this method reduces computational demand compared to full microscopic simulators like AIMSUN or CORSIM. Furthermore, we incorporate the effects of feedback-driven driver behaviors, such as route and departure time adjustments, and street lighting disruptions, which can induce varying volumes and travel time functions. Although these behaviors were originally developed for Mobility as a Service applications, they prove equally vital for time-dependent travel demand response. Finally, we extend an existing model-predictive control approach to regulate departing volumes, incorporating mainstreet traffic effects and feedback driver behaviors. Simulation results demonstrate that considering these factors can substantially alter achieved throughputs and underscore the necessity of including mainstreet effects, particularly when primary throughputs are high or when mainstreet congestion affects stored vehicle departures.

Although previous attempts have been made to incorporate time-dependent travel times and volumes into traffic simulation and control, significant shortcomings remain. This paper highlights these limitations and addresses them by integrating an arrival function and extending a cell transmission model to create a hybrid framework. This new system combines macroscopic and microscopic elements to forecast traveling and stored vehicle counts, thereby offering more accurate predictions of departing volumes under varying travel time and volume conditions. Subsequently, we utilize this hybrid model for traffic control that aims to prevent stored vehicle counts from exceeding specified limits. Our findings indicate that purely macroscopic models may substantially underestimate stored vehicles when travel times are highly time-dependent, and a method similar to our proposed hybrid model is necessary for effective traffic control.

While recent attempts have integrated physical knowledge into LSTM models, they typically rely on hand-crafted formulations that demand extensive prior knowledge. This limitation motivates our development of PhysForecast, the first model to learn the encoding of physical knowledge directly from data. Thermal states are fundamental to both theoretical understanding and experimental applications of quantum systems. While preparing these states for complex systems remains a significant challenge, our theoretical tools rely on formalism based on imaginary time evolution. This work introduces an account for noise effects in quantum thermalization, ensuring the accuracy of thermal state preparation and estimation.

Although quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) has been employed to approximate ground and thermal states for over a decade, its utility for complex systems is limited by noise sensitivity. We analyze these noise effects, extending the analysis beyond the standard noise-free scenario. Our investigation reveals that certain systems reach equilibrium under noisy conditions, a phenomenon not guaranteed in the absence of noise. Additionally, entangled measurements within QITE contribute to the many-body factorization of the density matrix, an effect that must be considered when estimating expectation values. To obtain accurate thermal state properties, we apply these insights to adjust QITE protocols for both ground and thermal states, using the Heisenberg picture for expectation value calculations. We validate our findings through various numerical examples, including systems where interacting Hamiltonians are expanded into sums of two-body terms for resolution via quantum coupled-cluster theory.

This paper presents an open-source, flexible simulation tool developed in Python to examine various design alternatives within both energy and capacity markets. The tool is built upon well-established microsimulation methods, offering a modular framework that streamlines the testing of design changes and computational techniques. It features a comprehensive suite of design options, ranging from bidding structures and unit characteristics to commitment rules and out contracts. Furthermore, the system supports design examinations through multiple contract signing methods, settlement procedures, and retirement mechanisms. By facilitating the investigation of existing and potential market architectures, this platform aims to aid regulators, policymakers, and industry participants in understanding market dynamics and the economic implications of design decisions. The code repository can be accessed at https://github.com/UCBerkeley-EE/PySim.

The electricity sector is increasingly dynamic due to climate change-driven demand shifts, rising integration of intermittent renewables like wind and solar, and the need to deploy new generation, storage, and demand-response technologies. While this transition presents challenges, it also offers opportunities to enhance reliability and lower costs for ratepayers and the economy. However, understanding these market dynamics and the impacts of policy decisions requires rigorous analysis of design features and operational mechanisms.

Although simulation models are vital for evaluating the effects of policy and design, current options are limited, and they often lack the necessary detail, flexibility, or transparency to effectively support policy assessment.

To address these issues, this report introduces a detailed description of the PySim platform, which was created to develop a robust set of simulation tools for the electricity sector. PySim is written in Python, a language renowned for its versatility, flexibility, and transparency.

PySim offers a detailed and adaptable method for exploring diverse aspects of electricity market design and operation. The platform supports a wide array of design elements, including auction types, bidding structures, contract types, marking-to-market practices, retirement and settlement procedures, and operational constraints. This framework enables the assessment of how these design choices influence market outcomes.

These features are connected to winter cold traps situated between 70° and 80° latitude. While Cassini captured the trap filling with air transported from lower latitudes, the vortices formed when these winter traps locked up large inventories of constituent gases during their respective seasons. We characterize these vortices and traps using three formation and maintenance mechanisms: 1) Sealed off-isobaric traps that fill with planetary flow transported gases and develop vortices when they spin up; 2) Sealed off-isentropic traps that accumulate transported gases and spawn vortices when heated across sufficient pressure depth; and 3) Vortices generated by the separation of incoming planetary flow inversely baroclinic to the mean state. The Cassini observations support the conclusion that off-isobaric traps dominate in the deeper atmosphere (pressures < 0.1 mbar), whereas off-isentropic traps dominate at shallower depths (pressures > 3 mbar). Additionally, the data suggest that not all vortices result from winter trap fill-ups; some are created by air separation processes. We also propose a new class of vortices formed by the accumulation of horizontally transported gases within off-isentropic traps that subsequently cool into visible vortices after being advected into the traps. This study confirms the fundamental role of sealed off-isobaric and off-isentropic traps in generating large warm vortices on hydrogen-helium gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, suggesting that accumulation traps may also explain the origin of Earth's Antarctic ozone hole.

Bayes factors are a pivotal tool for empiricist scientists to test scientific hypotheses. While they provide advantages over other methods, the lack of user-friendly packages hinders their adoption. To address this, we introduced the bayesfactor package, which allows researchers to compute Bayes factors for many common models without relying on potentially time-consuming MCMC methods.

To validate validity, one must ensure that a method adheres to its assumptions. Here, I examine the BayesFactor package's two-tailed t-test assumption using simulation. My findings indicate that the package fails to produce valid Bayes factors even with large sample sizes when comparing two means. The issue stems from an incorrect assumption regarding the sampling distribution of the Bayes factor for two-sample mean comparisons. Specifically, BayesFactor incorrectly assumes independence between the group means. Valid Bayes factors for this scenario require accounting for all four parameters (two per group); however, the package erroneously depends only on the two parameters defining the difference in group means.

The adoption of Bayes factors remains limited in many fields, including psychology, partly due to the absence of convenient software. ### Introduction

Backpropagation remains the most prevalent method for teaching trained artificial neural networks. By computing layer-by-layer gradients via the chain rule, it efficiently generates precise weight updates that enable high-performance processing. However, despite its artificial origins, backpropagation strikingly mirrors the operational mechanism of the brain: information flows forward during stimulation (similar to activity propagation), while teaching signals travel backward during learning (resembling a Hebbian process where pre- and post-synaptic activities determine learning directions). This coincidence suggests a potential convergence between biological and artificial learning systems, yet it creates a significant problem because backpropagation depends on storing global error values throughout the network—a requirement that demands an unrealistic amount of memory and direct supervision from external teachers for every neuron.

To resolve this contradiction, we seek a local learning algorithm that avoids global error storage and operates without external supervision, ideally matching the structural organization of the cerebral cortex. While many such local rules exist, none have previously achieved the training accuracy of backpropagation. This discrepancy is puzzling given that both approaches operate as non-convex optimization problems. Our prior research indicates that certain local learning algorithms can effectively tackle high-dimensional, non-convex challenges. Therefore, it is striking that backpropagation could potentially be replaced by a local learning rule within a properly designed neural network.

This study examines additional limitations arising from Supernova 1987A's non-detection of specific signals. If such particles were produced thermally in the core of SN 1987A, they could either decay into lighter particles within a detectable range or emit energy via GE. We investigate a mean-field opinion formation model featuring two agent types: those with fixed spins (the Ising model) and those who adjust their opinions ($\pm 1$) based on a majority vote among neighbors. When the concentration of Ising agents is sufficiently low, a new phase emerges where the system's steady state exhibits ordered opinions and hysteresis, contrasting with the democratic disordered state ($\langle m \rangle = 0$) found in the pure voter model. This phase transition is driven by the mutual irreversibility of agent interactions. Hysteresis displays multiple stable states determined by initial conditions and hysteresis loops with varying areas. In the ordered phase, the system's magnetization is predominantly determined by the agents' initial opinion distribution. Additionally, the mean activity—representing the fraction of agents changing opinions per unit time—shows a peak at the critical line separating the disordered and ordered phases, a phenomenon also observed in other nonequilibrium systems. We address two related challenges: (1) identifying efficient methods to derive meaningful accuracy guarantees for classifying convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and (2) determining how to leverage these guarantees to enhance a CNN's raw accuracy. Existing techniques for black-box models are either difficult to implement or produce excessively conservative bounds. Our solution involves analyzing the ReLU activation function's properties to construct a novel, efficient accuracy guarantee for classification CNNs (Theorem~\ref{thm:main}). We also develop a improvement algorithm (Algorithm~\ref{alg:main}) that utilizes these guarantees to maximize the network's raw accuracy. Our approach is applicable to any CNN with dropout, fully connected, or convolutional layers given query access to the black-box model. On the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, we confirm (1) that our accuracy guarantees significantly outperform previous methods and (2) that our improvement algorithm successfully raises both raw and guaranteed accuracy, even for models trained exclusively on labeled data or solely on unlabeled data.

We investigated the outcomes of a Dutch book formed on forecasts of daily police injuries in Santiago, Chile, which occurred at the height of the October 2019 protests. The closed positions in this market indicate that the forecast distributions align with official government estimates. However, we observed that the variance, along with the mean, increases as the protest rally count rises. This suggests a model where the forecast for total injuries is a sum of forecasts for injuries at individual protest locations, with the number of locations being proportional to the number of rallies. This framework may also apply to other social events involving either numerous independent actors or a large number of reportable occurrences. We present several models of rumor propagation and conflicting narratives to explain the flow of information behind these public forecasts. The primary finding is that the forecasts seem accurate only when protest activity is high. This points to the existence of multiple, competing narratives regarding the protests, where extreme income inequality explains the origin of the core complaint, but not the specific rumors driving daily actions. Consequently, public information during such turmoil is fragmented and often misleading. We suggest that prediction markets can help clarify the number of reportable events during such periods.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by defining a Hamiltonian with both cubic Fermi arcs and linear dispersion. We demonstrate that SHOWS supports fifth-order Hopf Fermi arcs, which can be observed through surface states on two slabs of the material with opposite chirals. Grid cells were discovered approximately ten years ago in the medial entorhinal cortex of rats, exhibiting distinct firing patterns that map to periodic locations within the surroundings. While these findings originally implied a role as a spatial metric, later research has produced a vast body of knowledge about grid cells and the neural networks in the parahippocampal-hippocampal area that generate them. This area has become a central focus in understanding the spatial brain. Many aspects of grid cell behavior remain unexplained, and they may also fulfill functions related to time and object representation. This survey paper provides a comprehensive overview of grid cell literature from the past decade. It covers essential characteristics, fundamental generating mechanisms, and potential roles in time estimation and object representation within the spatial brain. Additionally, significant directions for future research are identified. This survey serves as a fundamental introduction to grid cells for the broader field of the spatial brain. This approach yields an estimate of the entropies (relative to the base-2 logarithm) of the two least-populated eigenvalues of the states comprising the key, improving upon previous estimates that focused solely on the two largest eigenvalues. Such estimation is essential for determining whether secret key extraction is feasible when the total entropy of the two least-significant states falls between 2 and 3 bits. These variations are influenced by both internal processes, such as plate tectonics and volcanism, and external factors, including space weather generated by the interaction between a planet's magnetosphere and its magnetized solar wind. A critical gap in current understanding lies in the uncertain roles of these internal and external mechanisms in shaping the atmospheres of terrestrial and Mars-sized planets. This work reviews relevant literature to outline future research questions that could clarify these dynamics, potentially through data from upcoming in-situ and remote sensing missions. By applying a simple model of atmospheric mass balance, we quantify the influence of these factors across different planetary bodies, highlighting how their relative importance can vary significantly, which is essential for properly interpreting future atmospheric data. Finally, we explore how these insights can guide the design of upcoming investigations.

This research indicates how comparing the long-term atmospheric evolution of Venus, Mars, and Earth will help determine the origins of habitability and guide future studies.

Venus exhibits high atmospheric density alongside slow rotation and a lack of a global magnetic field, resulting in an atmosphere heavily shaped by atmospheric escape. While volcanic outgassing is recognized as the primary source of volatiles, both internal and external mechanisms contribute to loss. Although surface and atmospheric data from recent probes have clarified volatile inventories and composition, determining long-term evolution remains challenging, as has been the case for decades.

Mars, characterized by a thin, cold atmosphere and a weak global magnetic field, is thought to have been more dense and warm in its early history, potentially supporting liquid water. Like Venus, its current state reflects significant atmospheric loss, with internal and external factors playing comparable roles. However, the specific processes and their relative importance remain uncertain, necessitating data on the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in the atmosphere and crust, as well as the total volatile content of the planet.

Earth, uniquely protected by a global magnetic field that largely shields it from external atmospheric stripping, serves as a benchmark for internal versus external process dominance. Additionally, Earth offers opportunities to directly measure the rates of internal source processes.

Ultimately, a model of planetary atmospheric evolution is required to synthesize these source and loss processes and accurately interpret data from future in-situ and remote sensing missions.

In many applications, direct collocation proves highly effective for generating accurate numerical solutions to optimal control problems. This paper presents a new direct collocation formulation that enhances sparsity in the resulting nonlinear programming (NLP) formulation. This improved sparsity, coupled with an efficient KKT-based NLP solver, enables the solution of higher-fidelity problems that were previously computationally unattainable.

Recent advancements in parallel computing have significantly boosted the speed and accuracy with which nonlinear programming (NLP) formulations can be solved. This study reports successful applications of extended direct transcription to both a linear quadratic regulator and an interplanetary trajectory. The proposed direct transcription form increases solution sparsity, facilitating more efficient handling of constraints. This formulation is particularly well-suited for solving NLPs on recently introduced architectures, such as GPU processors.

Direct transcription methods are widely recognized for their simplicity and efficiency in addressing optimal control problems. This work further explores these methods by applying them to multi-shuttle spacecraft formations. A direct collocation form is derived that maximizes solution sparsity, and its performance is evaluated on NLP formulations governing relative dynamics expressed in relative and absolute Cartesian coordinates

**Motivation:** This study demonstrates that Transfer Learning, Data Adaptation, and Deep Transfer Learning are effective for cancer detection and classification.

This difficulty arises because such algorithms are heavily dependent on data distribution and can suffer performance declines when trained on one dataset and tested on another. Although data augmentation and transfer learning are potential solutions, they are limited by the scarcity of publicly available training data and the significant morphological and staining variations between datasets.

Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Multivariate point processes find applications in diverse fields such as social, economic, neuroscientific, and disaster-related event modeling. The Hawkes process, a type of self-exciting multivariate point process, is characterized by interactions that can be excitatory (increasing event probability) or inhibitory (decreasing it). This research concentrates on stopping times for the observation path of the Hawkes process. Specifically, we consider a scenario where all parameters of the process are estimated from data using a Gaussian process prior. We establish rates of convergence for the posterior estimates and leverage these to define a stopping time, demonstrating that the process remains well-defined up to this point. Additionally, we prove bounds on the conditional probability of future events given the current process state, highlighting the method's versatility for various prediction tasks.

Multivariate point processes are frequently employed to analyze sequences of discrete occurrences, such as social media interactions, code commits, financial trades, and neuronal spikes. The Hawkes process is a prominent model within this category, characterized by parameters that regulate event frequency and the nature of interactions, whether they are self-, cross-, or multivariate, and if they are excitatory or inhibitory. This paper concentrates on the Hawkes process and addresses two challenges: ensuring the process is mathematically well-defined and creating a temporary "quiet period" where no events can occur. Achieving this involves estimating the parameters from data via Gaussian process regression and determining a stopping time based on the resulting posterior process. The study presents findings regarding the convergence of this posterior process to the true process and the behavior of the stopping time.

This reliance creates a specific vulnerability known as "label shift," where minor deviations in data distribution can severely compromise model performance. Drawing inspiration from copy editing, we propose a framework for "label-free diagnosis," which utilizes a "verified positive" distribution to constrain and enhance CNN predictions. Our method, termed "distribute learning," trains the network to align its output probability alignment with this verified positive distribution. We demonstrate that label-free diagnosis effectively mitigates label shift, outperforming various state-of-the-label techniques on corrupted datasets. Consequently, our framework offers a robust solution for disease detection that is particularly advantageous in resource-constrained settings where obtaining clean labels is difficult. Code and results are accessible at https://github.com/19961103/distribute_learning.

We investigate the impact of labels with a bias toward verified positives on deep neural network training. Contrary to expectations, we find that these biased labels can be as effective as fully correct labels for training classification models to identify positive instances, a phenomenon we term "half labels." This approach is particularly useful when only a subset of labels is confirmed, such as in "disease present" classifications. We introduce a method for optimizing neural networks using these partially biased labels, demonstrating its superiority over several existing methods through experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. Our source code can be found at https://github.com/19961103/HalfLabels.

Deep learning models for disease detection often fail to generalize to data with slight distributional shifts, a challenge that becomes even more pronounced when training data exhibits label noise. This study evaluates various label-noise-tolerant methods, including co-teaching, parametric noise-contrastive estimation, and label biasing, against a standard cross-entropy baseline on both natural and disease-specific datasets. Natural datasets were modified to simulate label noise at different rates and distribution shifts, while disease-specific datasets were created to mimic labeling errors in clinical reports. Results indicate that the label bias method outperforms all others, maintaining performance close to the clean-label baseline across most experimental conditions. Future work will focus on developing more sophisticated frameworks for label bias to further improve disease detection accuracy.

### Introduction

Individuals with chronic conditions often require routine monitoring to manage their health and avert severe complications. Clinical data sources, such as electronic health records (EHRs), facilitate this process by offering insights into disease progression and enabling providers to adjust care plans. For instance, patients with diabetes can be assessed for retinopathy risk through dilated eye exams; detecting early signs allows for timely interventions that can prevent vision loss.

Despite the clear benefits of integrating real-world data for risk assessment and prevention, obstacles exist in accessing external information. A patient visiting a primary care clinic for an annual checkup may not have recent laboratory results available within that system.

In many scenarios, text-based social determinants of health (SDoH) can be incorporated into risk models without compromising patient privacy. This report examines whether adding SDoH data to risk models improves predictions

We explicitly address and solve two optimal control problems: minimizing travel time and minimizing quadratic cost to move the swimmer between fixed positions using periodic control. By considering a single dynamic switch and leveraging the motion equations' decomposition into two separate fluid regimes, we reduce the problem of finding an optimal control to comparing the solutions of two linear optimal control problems. Additionally, we compare the computational complexities of addressing the restricted single-switch case versus the general multi-switch scenario. This comparison highlights the significant computational advantages of the approach utilizing a single switch, offering a practical and efficient strategy for resolving such bilateral control problems. The findings presented in this work on the two simple cases also serve to correct an error found in the literature. This research constitutes a critical step toward understanding the dynamics and optimality of the classic undulated eel model. Finally, the framework and methods established in this study on the two simple cases can be adapted to analyze similar scenarios involving other biological organisms, such as the eight-legged desert animal *Eumorphophoetus elegans*, which also exhibits a transition between two distinct fluid regimes. In that specific case, however, the general multi-switch problem would yield the optimal control due to its structure. Ultimately, the framework from this study provides a framework for determining the existence of an optimal control for the undulated eel model.

The desert animal *Eumorphophoetus elegans*, which possesses eight legs, moves by switching between two distinct fluid dynamics regimes. This study considers an idealized model of this creature and addresses the task of minimizing a quadratic cost function over a fixed duration. The analysis involves a transition between two systems of nonlinear ordinary differential differential describing the organism's motion within these differing fluid environments. The solution to the corresponding Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation confirms the existence of an optimal control comprising a single switch between the two dynamic systems. The timing of this switch is directly proportional to the initial velocity of the animal. These findings on *E. elegans* also imply the existence of an optimal control for the simpler two-link undulated eel model.

The primary objective is to characterize how uniform shear flow influences the modulation of weakly nonlinear, quasi-monochromatic surface gravity waves. By employing Hamiltonian transformation theory on the Hamiltonian formulation of the system, we derive a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation governing the temporal evolution of the wave envelope. Consistent with prior findings, our results indicate that the impact of uniform shear flow on the modulational instability of Stokes waves varies based on the flow's direction and magnitude, either enhancing or suppressing the instability. Furthermore, our approach offers a non-perturbative method to reconstruct surface elevation from the wave envelope, utilizing a Birkhoff normal form transformation to remove all non-resonant triads. The validity of this model is confirmed through comparisons with direct numerical simulations of the full water wave equations, both with and without the influence of uniform shear flow. Additionally, we demonstrate that the conserved Hamiltonian of the Dysthe equation accurately predicts the combined energy of bound states and breathers, which were previously identified through direct numerical simulations. Bondi-Coppola bound states are also examined in detail, revealing that their energy partition between bound and free states depends on the direction of the uniform shear current. Finally, the study concludes by extending the analysis to weakly nonlinear waves featuring a prescribed horizontal current. This extension establishes a one-to-one mapping between the Goldstein equation and the Dressen-Farrell equation, highlighting that bound states exist exclusively in subcritical flow regimes. These results significantly extend the classical El'coviski-Craig-Yu solution to incorporate weak nonlinearity.
Surface water bodies subject to varying bottom topographies support surface gravity waves whose behavior is fundamentally altered by such interactions. We formulate a generalized Hamiltonian framework for surfaces with constant curvature (flat or spherical) and arbitrary bottoms to derive a boundary integral model capable of capturing weakly nonlinear, surface-trapped wave dynamics. Building on Bondara's work, we explicitly express the model's variables in terms of the velocity potential at an arbitrary fixed depth, thereby establishing an exact equivalence between the two formulations. Utilizing a multiple scales perturbation method, we develop a Newell-Whitehead-Whitehead (NWW) equation to describe the evolution of weakly nonlinear, nearly monochromatic waves. Based on the specific Hamiltonian derived, we demonstrate that both supercritical and subcritical flow regimes can arise depending on the water depth, thereby influencing the existence of bound states and the presence of a soliton hump. We characterize the echo chamber effect as a phenomenon where, for any text, the probability of a user sharing the text is significantly influenced by the proportion of users who share the same sentiment and tone as the author. We present a machine learning-based approach for quantifying this phenomenon. We constructed a novel **Twitter-based YouTube (TWY) dataset** from Twitter and YouTube comments to collect labels for training and testing. We generated a second dataset, the **YouTube Word (YWD) dataset**, from YouTube comments to validate our method's feasibility on large-scale, unfamiliar data sources. We compared our method against state-of-the-art techniques for echo chamber detection. Our methods outperformed these comparisons, and the evaluation on the YWD dataset confirms the feasibility of reverberation scoring for echo chamber detection in large-scale, unseen data. Our proposed method enables the assignment of echo chamber scores to individual social media posts, which can be utilized for filtering, ranking, or warning users. Additionally, the quantification of this effect allows users to better understand and control their information consumption.

Secrecy remains a critical concern in multiple access systems, particularly when utilizing multiple-input multiple-output techniques such as orthogonal multiple access (OMA), space division multiple access (SDMA), and nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA). In OMA, users are grouped into orthogonal sets, with the system's overall throughput and potential secure throughputs contingent upon the selection of an optimal set and a corresponding coding scheme. In contrast, SDMA transmits signals to all users simultaneously without orthogonality, requiring a precoding matrix to ensure each user can decode its own data. NOMAM, a specific type of SDMA, was examined in this paper. Within NOMAM, all users share a common codebook, and the precoding matrix is crafted so that each user can successfully decode its intended message while treating the interference from other users' messages as noise to maintain security.

This paper focuses on ensuring security in NOMAM by analyzing two key metrics: the total number of possible decoding orders and those that guarantee a positive secrecy rate for all untrusted users. We evaluate a method to quantify these feasible decoding orders, along with a suboptimal strategy to select the order that maximizes total secure throughout. Our results indicate that in a system with three users, the feasible decoding orders account for approximately 67% of all possible orders. With four users, this proportion rises to about 75%.

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA), a robust alternative to conventional PCA, has gained significant popularity in recent years. This study examines a rotationally invariant variant of L1-PCA, which remains largely unexplored in existing literature. To address this challenge, we introduce a proximal alternating linearized minimization method incorporating nonlinear extrapolation to solve the problem's two-block reformulation. We further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges to a critical point of its reformulated problem, which corresponds to a critical point of the original problem due to their equivalence. Numerical experiments conducted across synthetic and real-world datasets validate the problem setting, the convergence analysis, and the overall approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Amirhamedarshadi/RI-L1-PCA.

Outlier detection and dimensionality reduction remain critical yet unresolved challenges in current research. This paper presents a dimensionality reduction framework based on a robust, rotationally invariant extension of weighted least-squares. We prove the method's convergence to a critical point by utilizing a reformulated optimization problem and a tailored proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm with nonlinear extrapolation. Furthermore, we establish global convergence for specific rank and weight restrictions by analyzing the reformulated problem's Hessian matrix at critical points. The approach was tested on both synthetic and real-world datasets, with source code available at https://github.com/Amirhamedarshadi/WR0-LS-PCA.

Finding a robust, globally convergent dimensionality reduction method for data with anomalies is a significant yet difficult task in dimensionality reduction research. Outlier- and noise-resistant least-squares techniques often struggle to global convergence due to nonconvexity introduced by robustity and rotation invariance. This paper proposes a direct extension of such a technique. We analyze the Hessian matrix of a reformulated objective function to guarantee global convergence. We also discuss integrating data weights and demonstrate how our method relates to principal curves in high-dimensional space. Experimental results were obtained from synthetic and real-world datasets.

Achieving global convergence in dimensionality reduction using robust, rotationally invariant least-squares methods is challenging due to the nonconvexity of the associated optimization problem. This paper offers global convergence guarantees by restricting the number of principal components and proving that, under certain conditions, the objective function possesses a unique global minimizer. We compare this global solution with local minimizers found using a reformulated objective function and standard algorithms

We also provide release instructions for two new ML models trained on this dataset to support subsequent secondary tasks. **Note on Data Accessibility:**
While we strived to maximize data volume, a significant portion of the potential dataset remained unannotated due to the limitations imposed by our human annotators. This limitation stems from the very feature we sought to highlight: the ability of NLP models to assist in identifying "keyness." The efficacy of BERT in predicting keyness, as demonstrated in this release, allows annotators to quickly grasp the relevance of specific segments, thereby significantly reducing the time required for annotation.

To achieve this, we define a novel category of prefix-independent bi-positional winning conditions known as energy conditions, which are based on totally ordered groups. We demonstrate this refutation by presenting a specific non-energy condition called the root condition. Our analysis relies on a core tool, the Parity index of an infinite game, which allows us to construct counterexamples to Kopczyński's conjecture. These systems are defined by a white dwarf spin period that deviates slightly (typically by a few percent) from the binary orbital period, being either faster or slower. Their disproportionate detection in soft gamma-ray surveys has prompted speculation that they possess intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. By comparing asynchronous and standard polars to investigate the link between synchronization status and spectral morphology, our analysis of the full asynchronous polar sample suggests they may indeed exhibit harder spectra, though this finding lacks statistical significance. Furthermore, we investigated whether the direction of spin synchronization (faster vs. slower) correlates with the chemical composition of the accreted material or the log(g) value, again finding no significant results. A Bayesian analysis of the data successfully recovered the two distinct populations of faster and slower spinning polars. We identified a potential correlation between an asymptotic log(g) value and the direction of synchronization, though this also remains statistically unconfirmed. Finally, by modeling the spin synchronization timescale ($\tau_{sync}$) based on the accretion rate ($\dot{M}$) and a power-law dependency on the mass accretion radius ($R_{ma}$), we derived that $R_{ma}$ varies with accretion rate as $R_{ma} \propto \dot{M}^{-0.6}$. This derived slope is consistent with, though not strictly limited to, a supercritical disk configuration. As a byproduct, we determined the inclination angles for five additional asynchronous polars whose values had not been previously reported. With an total sample of 26 systems, this work significantly expands the available data on these enigmatic systems. The derived supercritical disk model, characterized by a three-lobed structure, may offer a unified explanation for the spectral differences observed between asynchronous and standard polars.
