While most existing map representations depend on drift-free state estimation to generate global metric maps, maintaining such consistency and speed is challenging in large-scale real-world scenarios. This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel representation designed to improve upon current methods. Its core concept involves utilizing a submap-based hierarchical topology instead of a global metric map, thereby maintaining only local metric maps for obstacle avoidance and ensuring the system remains lightweight. To facilitate exploration of unknown areas, frontiers are identified and integrated into the map as attributes. Furthermore, a path planning module was developed to assess the feasibility and efficiency of this representation. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through both simulation and real-world testing, and the HiTMap implementation is released as open-source. Consequently, HiTMap represents a more efficient solution for map-based autonomous navigation in unknown environments, offering a valuable tool for developing reliable mobile robotic systems. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/HuaweiHiTMap/HiTMap. The corresponding simulation environment can be found at: http://hitmap.mrlabs.hust.edu.cn/.
Mobile robotics typically employs simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) to determine the agent's position and construct an environment representation, which is essential for navigation in unknown spaces. However, the reliance on a globally consistent, exact map—maintained to prevent particle filter degeneracy in Gaussian mixture maps or to ensure accurate pose estimation in other frameworks—creates a significant burden, as continuous refinement of every observed location is computationally prohibitive and prone to accumulating drift. This work presents a lightweight alternative called Frontier-based Hierarchical Map (FHM) specifically for exploration tasks. The FHM consists of two main components: a graph of submaps linked by a hierarchical topology, and an attached list of frontiers—areas not yet observed or occupied. A log map is included to support these features. A simultaneous path planning module was implemented to ensure the map remains current and to validate its performance. Experimental results from both simulation and physical hardware confirm the efficiency, effectiveness, and reliability of this approach. The source code is available at: https://github.com/HuaweiHiTMap/FHM.

In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. This approach paves the way for future atomic measurements of the magnetic flux generated by the electron's spin magnetic moment. Additionally, the technique of detecting weak local fields through the expulsion effect may be applied to other contexts, such as detecting weak gravitational fields using a superconducting ball instead of atoms in an atomic interferometer. Although the giant magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in bulk materials has enabled powerful magnetic refrigeration, miniaturizing this phenomenon into 2D systems remains challenging due to the difficulty of generating substantial entropy changes in low-dimensional structures. Additionally, we show that both the maximum MCE and the entropy change are highly sensitive to the thickness of the TMD layer.

Strong normalization—the guarantee that terms within a formal system do not engage in infinite reduction sequences—is a defining characteristic of the Calculus of Constructions (Coquand 1980). This work examines three proofs of this property for CC: the initial demonstration by Coquand (1980), the revised approach by Thierry (1993), and the recent re-imagining by Daniel (2019). By analyzing the shared foundations of these methods while clarifying their distinct modifications, we situate these proofs within a geometric type theory perspective (2016). This framework serves as a unifying lens to understand their fundamental mechanisms. Although the proofs are distinct, they all rely on a reformulation of the emptiness of excutability (Daniel 2016a), which ensures strong normalization for a broader class of extended Calculi of Constructions.

This paper extends our prior survey (Daniel 2016; Daniel 2016a) to access a wider audience, covering the same material but incorporating additional explanations, references, and examples. To develop software that is both robust and efficient, programmers must also adhere to programmatic principles rooted in formal logic. Despite this, many current programming languages and their associated ecosystems overemphasize object models, often to the detriment of code maintainability.

To address this imbalance, we propose a balanced method grounded in second-order logic that unifies program correctness with object-oriented design. Our approach places data types at the core of software architecture, treating classes as instances of types and messages as functions. By doing so, it eliminates the need for complex mechanisms such as inheritance, polymorphism, and dynamic binding.

We have implemented this method in a new language called OOL (Object-Oriented Logic). In demonstrations using this language, we show how to build software that is straightforward to construct, rigorous, highly reliable, and fully backward compatible with existing systems. The source code for OOL is publicly available at github.com/ozkara/OOL.

We contend that software development would be significantly more effective if practitioners were provided with tools and ecosystems that prioritize programmatic qualities—包括 maintainability, robustness, and correctness—over an excessive focus on object-oriented abstractions.

Since the introduction of Simula in the 1960s, inheritance has been a cornerstone feature of most programming languages. While often celebrated for enabling code modularity and reducing redundancy, we argue that these benefits are better achieved through careful software design within languages that lack inheritance. Furthermore, we demonstrate how a logical foundation can yield a practical, object-like language that supports many contemporary object-oriented concepts—including message passing, encapsulation, and reflection—without requiring inheritance, recursion, or self.

Although modern software systems are vast and intricate, making it difficult to assess the prevalence and impact of specific features, our analysis of nearly 20,000 open-source Python packages reveals a significant reliance on inheritance. Approximately 20% of all classes utilize inheritance, with 1% relying on multi-level hierarchies and 1% on recursive definitions. Although Python was not originally designed for inheritance, 80% of its classes are crafted to be free of it.

The finite-size corrections to the muonic g-2 value ($a_\mu$) represent a significant component of the discrepancy between measurement and theory in the muon anomaly. These corrections are primarily determined by the root-mean-square charge and matter radii of the atomic nucleus. While the charge radius of nuclei can be precisely measured experimentally, the matter radius remains largely unknown for most heavy nuclei. Moreover, the matter radius is intrinsically linked to the nuclear interaction, specifically the short-distance behavior of the nuclear wave function, which is often input into shell-model calculations as low-momentum interactions derived from realistic nucleon-nucleon potentials. ### 1 Introduction

Instance segmentation is a computer vision task that requires models to identify and localize every occurrence of a specific class within an image. Despite decades of research, accurately segmenting instances at high resolution remains challenging. Although the field has largely relied on CNN-based methods utilizing extensive annotated datasets, recent advances in deep learning have introduced implicit neural representations. These models map input coordinates to output values via parameterized function approximators, often achieving favorable results with minimal training data. Building on this, we develop an method (see Section 2) that leverages implicit functions to predict instance masks.

Existing methods like Sinusoidal Encoding Networks (SINE) have demonstrated the potential of implicit representations by rendering 3D scenes from sparse views. Similarly, MipMask showed that inverting an implicit function could render images from masked scene representations. We build upon these techniques to address instance segmentation.

This report details the final technical and managerial phases of the FIRST project, which ran from November 1, 2016, to October 31, 2019, with a total duration of 48 months. The study examines a specific anomaly observed during the first month of operations at the LHC: a notable increase in single particle losses at injection following heavy ion collisions at the LHC colliders. Shifting to plasma physics, the report introduces a mechanism explaining this anomaly: a chirped laser pulse can trigger a self-consistent chirped plasma expansion, potentially accounting for the anomalous transmission of high-intensity, chirped pulses through sub-critical plasma. Additionally, the report presents a proposed X-ray pump-probe setup where pumping a positively charged plasma foil with a chirped laser (after initial pre-conditioning) can generate an ultra-bright, sub-femtosecond, ultra-violet, or soft X-ray pulse. Finally, the document outlines both near-future and long-term applications, emphasizes the experiment's feasibility given current global capabilities, and lists potential extensions, including schemes to significantly boost X-ray intensity. These extensions involve chirping plasmas rather than just lasers or using dual chirped plasmas, concepts made possible by the insights gained from the FIRST project. The report concludes by providing relevant references.

detecting elastic top-quark pair production at the LHC via forward proton tagging, a process that remains closed off to other channels at current thresholds. The analysis demonstrates that the elastic cross section exceeds the inelastic one for transverse masses above 3 TeV, indicating that proton remnant effects can be neglected in elastic scattering. Based on this finding, a formula is derived that corrects the approximate elastic cross-to-total cross ratio to all orders. Consequently, the maximum mass reachable in the elastic channel for a given forward proton tag momentum is no longer a function of the total top-quark cross section. It is further shown that the forward proton tag momentum can be measured with high precision, as the uncertainty contributes less than 1% to the maximum mass for a 1% uncertainty in the total cross section. This method enables an increase in the accessible mass range by approximately 10% to 1 TeV, extending the search into the closed-inelastic regime. The proposed approach is highly sensitive to all new physics contributing to elastic top-quark pair production, including resonances, and can determine their properties with statistical significance comparable to existing methods. The strategy remains viable even if new physics generates only a 10% correction to the total cross section at the resonance mass. Additionally, the derived maximum mass formula can serve as a benchmark for future hadron colliders, such as the HL-LHC or the FCC, in searches for resonant top quark pair production. Finally, the protocol may be adaptable to other final states, including Higgs-boson pair and $W$-boson pair production.
This document details the parameters and assumptions of a machine-learning model trained to identify anomalous jet substructure signatures of heavy resonances decaying into top-quark pairs. While many prior studies focus on total decay energy, this model utilizes angular variables, specifically the top-quark pair rapidity and the angle between top quarks in their rest frame relative to the lab frame. Using Monte Carlo simulations, an upper bound on the mass of a narrow, top-quark pair-resonance is established such that the model can detect anomalies up to an excess of five standard deviations beyond a mass of 5.3 TeV. The discussion extends to how the model might identify lower-mass resonances, noting that while the exact reachable mass depends on specific beyond-the-standard-model scenarios, it could potentially exceed 1.5 TeV, corresponding to a 3.5 sigma signal in the current LHC data.

This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with a vertex set possessing an upper density of at least $\lambda$, for a given finite graph $F$. We establish a novel lower bound for this problem; for specific graphs $F$, including cliques and odd cycles, this bound is optimal as it aligns with a previously known upper bound. Furthermore, in the specific instance where $F$ is a triangle, we provide an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \approx 0.62203$, which surpasses the earlier best result of $3/5$. The proof strategy involves novel applications of the Hales-Jewett theorem and the Ham Sandwich theorem. A significant component of our approach is a general lemma suitable for various $F$-Ramsey problems involving upper densities, of which our main theorem is a specific instance. We demonstrate this by deriving a result for odd cycles that improves upon prior work by György Elekes. Additionally, we extend Elekes's findings to the context of bounded degrees, though the primary focus of this study remains on upper densities. Notably, the main theorem holds true for general graphs, whereas the result derived from Elekes's work applies exclusively to trees. Regarding the corresponding lower bound problem, we direct readers to the thesis of György Kónig at https://hk.mtaif.klte.hu/konig-thesis.pdf. Leveraging the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy (ATLASGAL), we have generated a catalog of 2,555 dust condensations, or cores, within the CMZ. Utilizing known physical relationships between dust emission wavelengths, we derived estimates for the mass, radius, and peak temperature of these cores, and analyzed how these properties vary with galactic radius. We found that the cores' mass varies significantly, ranging from $0.027$ to $32.377$ M$_{\odot}$, while their radius ranges from 0.023 to 0.733 pc. The peak temperature spans between 7.6 K and 27.1 K. Statistical analyses were conducted by dividing the cores into groups based on these characteristics and their positions relative to the CMZ's major axis. On the inner side of this axis, the average mass is 2.37 M$_{\odot}$, compared to 1.17 M$_{\odot}$ on the outer side; similarly, the average radius is 0.25 pc on the inner side versus 0.18 pc on the outer side. Core density varies considerably, from $8.56$ to $1.04\times10^{5}$ cm$^{-3}$, with a mean density of $1.63\times10^{5}$ cm$^{-3}$. We observe that patient videos often lack clear markers of the disorder, whereas healthy subjects' videos contain distinct, detectable actions. Leveraging this insight, we developed a subject-independent approach to identify the disease. The subject-dependent stage involves training action recognition models to detect specific activities in subject videos, which are used to infer that the subject is healthy if any activity is found. Bell's Palsy, a temporary facial paralysis, is caused by inflammation in the facial nerve. Our approach involves training action recognition models in two phases: first, a subject-dependent stage to detect activities in subject (healthy individual) videos to confirm their healthy status; second, a subject-independent stage to detect Bell's Palsy across subjects using the outputs from the dependent phase. While many current methods struggle with variability among patients, our method offers a simple, effective, and subject-independent solution for detecting the condition.

We investigate the real-time dynamics of a non-Abelian SU(2) Heisenberg spin chain following both global and local quenches, comparing results from time evolution on finite chains, renormalization group methods, and thermofield dynamics. For global quenches, we observe that the entanglement growth between two halves of the chain starts linearly in time due to ballistic excitation propagation, transitioning to area law behavior at large times. In contrast, locally excited spin chains exhibit purely logarithmic entanglement growth at all times. These theoretical predictions were validated using an existing trapped-ion quantum computer platform. While the global quenche experiments aligned well with both infinite system approximations and bulk spectrum calculations, the local quenche experiment revealed larger deviations from theory and time numerics than expected. We attribute this discrepancy to excitation effects outside the two-magnon manifold, suggesting that the current setup effectively handles only the simplest local states. We also touch upon the feasibility of observing universal local quantum dynamics in other trapped-ion systems. Preprint: arXiv.org/2202.03311.

In this work, assuming $|S|$ is fixed, we identify groups $G$ with maximal diameter $diam(G,S)$ when $G$ possesses a specific group-theoretic property. Our primary findings are as follows: First, if $G$ has a non-cyclic abelian base of length $k$, then the groups with the largest possible diameter are the cyclic groups $C_{s^k}$, where $s=|S|$. Second, if $G$ is solvable but not abelian, the groups with the greatest diameter are the cyclic groups $C_{s^n}$, where $n$ is defined by $s+1 \le n \le 2s-2$. Third, if $G$ is non-solvable, then $diam(G,S)$ is bounded above by $|G:s|^2(s+1)$, where $s=|S|$. Consequently, in this scenario, the maximum diameter is a polynomial function of $|S|$, implying that no single group achieves a strictly maximal diameter. These results clarify which groups hold the record for diameter and demonstrate that such groups must be abelian. Our approach relies on establishing bounds for the diameter of groups based on the length of their abelian and solvable bases, as well as the maximum degree of a permutation representation arising from actions on cosets of maximal subgroups. This research is motivated by the Diameter Problem, a longstanding question in group theory seeking an upper bound for the diameter of groups $G$ with a fixed size generating set $S$ in terms of $|S|$, a problem that has seen significant recent activity. , and neutron stars are recognized for their long-term stability, yet the internal physical mechanisms sustaining them remain a subject of debate, particularly regarding the influence of stellar evolution. While analytical models generally assume magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium with magnetic fields confined by magnetic flux tubes, they often fail to fully incorporate magnetic anisotropy and may not achieve mathematical convergence beyond specific magnetic field strengths. Furthermore, these models lack a foundation in variational principles, meaning they cannot guarantee the minimization of magnetic free energy. In contrast, our comprehensive numerical approach addresses these gaps by utilizing a finite element method to solve a system of elliptic partial differential equations derived from the variational formulation of magnetoelasticity. This approach incorporates magnetic anisotropy and magneto-thermal coupling to explicitly account for magnetic phase transitions, thereby establishing a comprehensive framework for magnetic stellar structure calculations. This method is broadly applicable to various magnetic field topologies, including dipolar, toroidal, and mixed configurations. By establishing an iterative scheme that integrates the direct solution of magnetoelasticity with magnetic field relaxation, we enable the direct comparison of magnetic field energies across different topologies within the context of magnetic stellar structure. Our results indicate that for a given field strength, magnetic flux is not completely isolated from the surrounding plasma; instead, magnetoelastic stresses promote mixing between confined flux and ambient matter. Additionally, our study of magnetic white dwarfs reveals significant differences in internal structure and composition compared to non-magnetic counterparts, suggesting that stronger magnetic fields could potentially halt stellar contraction. These findings offer a robust framework for further investigating the interaction between magnetism and the evolution of chemically homogeneous Ap-stars, as well as the distinct origins of magnetic white dwarfs and neutron stars. Additionally, this work paves the way for exploring the impact of magnetic fields on the chemical segregation of inverted magnetic white dwarfs and the stability of rapidly rotating magnetic white dwarfs. Ultimately, this comprehensive approach serves as an essential foundation for a future population synthesis of magnetic white dwarfs and neutron stars. Additionally, we demonstrate how to incorporate a self-consistent wind model into this framework, providing a pathway to model the wind ablation of magnetized white dwarf atmospheres and potentially explaining the accumulation of hydrogen-rich envelopes.

Its utility is particularly notable for exploring systems that lack analytical solvability or adequate approximations, such as those without a small coupling constant. To achieve this, FRG employs a coarse-graining procedure analogous to the Wilsonian approach, integrating out high-momentum degrees of freedom to generate an infinite set of flow equations for effective field theories. This tutorial begins with field theories featuring a local Gaussian fixed point, where theoretical insights are established, analytical solutions exist, and interpretations are more straightforward. This tutorial is designed to complement the material presented in reference [1].

This paper introduces a simplified functional renormalization group (FRG) framework, illustrated first with solvable examples and subsequently applied to fields on curved manifolds or those exhibiting fundamental anti-periodicity in imaginary time. The FRG utilizes a coarse-graining procedure to integrate high-momentum degrees of freedom, creating flow equations that describe how couplings in the effective field theory evolve with the momentum scale. While powerful, the method is not without limitations. When applied to theories at a local Gaussian fixed point, the FRG demonstrates clear advantages over other standard techniques because these theories are analytically solvable, possess a well-defined local action, and are generally easier to interpret. However, these benefits diminish with theories at a nonlocal Gaussian fixed point, where fractal dimensions complicate action definitions and theoretical interpretation. By examining these contrasting cases, the method's utility is clarified. Advanced cases are discussed in [2]. Specifically, solvable field theories at a local Gaussian fixed point include:
1.  A harmonic oscillator, which demonstrates how the quantum Fractal dimension emerges from the theory's fundamental time anti-periodicity.
2.  Free bosons and free fermions, where the lack of such a dimension allows analytical treatment, and interpretations remain simple due to their fundamental locality.
In contrast, a harmonic oscillator at a nonlocal Gaussian fixed point represents a theory with a nonlocal action, where analytical solutions are unavailable and interpretations are markedly difficult.

This paper investigates the algebraic and relational semantics of G\"odel modal logics by utilizing the duality between finite G\"odel algebras and finite forests, defined as finite posets where principal downsets are totally ordered. We examine various subvarieties of the basic variety of G\"odel algebras with two modal operators (GAOs) and their associated classes of forest frames, featuring either single or dual accessibility relations. These relational structures function as prelinear adaptations of standard relational semantics for intuitionistic modal logic. Specifically, we analyze two primary extensions of finite G\"odel algebras with operators: one derived from adding Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intuitionistic logic fragments, and another based on Fischer Servi axioms. Furthermore, we establish J\'onsson-Tarski-style representation theorems for the distinct types of finite GAOs addressed in this study. Finally, we derive decidability results for the corresponding logical systems by leveraging the structural properties of their relational semantics. This work extends and updates research previously presented in the authors' conference paper [7].**Abstract**: G\"odel modal logics represent the primary extension of intuitionistic modal logics via the inclusion of a prelinearity axiom. This paper explores the relationships between the algebraic and relational semantics of finite G\"odel algebras with one or two modal operators and their respective axiomatic systems. Considered are four categories of G\"odel algebras with unified or separated accessibility relations, encompassing Dunn and Fischer Servi axioms. By applying standard representation theorems for G\"odel algebras and their relational counterparts as forests, we derive results on the decidability of the associated logics. This research extends and supersedes the findings of our conference paper [7].**Keywords**: G\"odel algebras, accessibility relations, Prelinear lattices, Forests, Decidability.

However, deriving accurate, continuous biomass maps from sparse 3D data remains challenging due to the high dimensionality of ecosystem data and the sparseness of LiDAR point clouds. To address this, we developed DeepBi, a convolutional neural network framework designed to predict continuous biomass values from sparse LiDAR data across varying data granularities. Our results demonstrate that DeepBi effectively learns spatial dependencies in vegetation structure from coarse to fine scales, producing accurate biomass estimates even from very sparse LiDAR returns. Specifically, for the sphere ${\mathbb S}^{d-1} \subset {\mathbb R}^d$, the strict positive definiteness of a zonal function $f(\cos \theta)$ is governed by the signs of the coefficients in its expansion using Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$, where $\lambda=(d-2)/2$. While recent findings indicate that classical differentiation and integration preserve positive definiteness in this setting, these operations shift the space dimension in increments of two. This paper introduces operators for zonal functions on the sphere that maintain positive definiteness without altering the associated dimension. These novel operators mimic fractional behavior with respect to zonal functions and can be iterated to generate a broad class of such functions. The resulting class, $\mathcal R$, encompasses Gegenbauer polynomials, sine and cosine, $\exp(if \cdot)$, fractional powers $|f|^\alpha$, and Bessel functions $J_\nu(f \cdot)$. Furthermore, the study examines the strict positive definiteness of Zernike polynomials, sine and cosine, and the fractional Zernike disk polynomials within this framework. The proposed framework holds promise for extending to other symmetric spaces, potentially yielding identities similar to those of Zernike disk polynomials for quadrature rules on spheres, as demonstrated in prior work by the authors. The findings are relevant to fields such as geophysics, atmospheric science, image analysis, machine learning, and control theory.

The fields of signal processing and harmonic analysis on the disk $\mathbb D$ and the sphere $\mathbb S^ {d-1}$ are interconnected through the projection established by the Stokes formula. This paper defines a class of functions, $\mathcal{M}$, consisting of holomorphic functions on the disk that are bounded, Zernike positive definite, and exhibit definite correlation with a point. By leveraging the correspondence between Zernike polynomials and Gegenbauer polynomials, we derive a representation of $\mathcal{M}$ based on its generating functions. This representation is then utilized to define a corresponding class of functions, $\mathcal{M}^*$, on the sphere. The representation of $\mathcal{M}^*$ involves fractional integration, a operation that does not change the fractal dimension of a surface. Consequently, a function in $\mathcal{M}^*$ retains its Zernike positive definiteness

-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major unsolved challenge in high-energy astrophysics. A promising strategy to address this mystery involves correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, as neutrinos directly trace hadronic interactions and remain unaffected by magnetic deflection. This paper outlines three distinct methods for correlating the arrival directions of these particles. Data were drawn from the 2018 IceCube high-energy neutrino catalog, which includes 95 events with energies exceeding 270 TeV and 95% confidence level error circles, and from the Telescope Array (TA) collaboration, covering a 37.5 degree² sky area with energy estimates above 40 EeV. To assess significance, we applied the HiCorr multi-hypothesis correlation framework, adapting it to the specific energy resolutions and error characteristics of both neutrino and UHECR datasets. Our results indicate no significant UHECR-neutrino correlations in any of the tested hypotheses. Notably, a strong sub-signal was detected when comparing TA UHECRs to IceCube neutrinos when employing a linear significance metric and a 0.25 degree correlation radius; this signal vanishes completely when quadratic significance metrics or smaller correlation radii are used. This discrepancy suggests a potential astrophysical connection, though it may also stem from statistical fluctuations, small sample sizes, or specific flavor compositions. To help guide future investigations, we provide an open-source implementation of HiCorr at http://cosmocraft.org/uhecr-neutrino-correlation/. Finally, we discuss how upcoming experiments and refined analysis techniques will advance this field in the future.

Context: Correlating neutrino and UHECR arrival directions remains a critical area of research in high-energy astrophysics. Previous attempts to identify a connection between a IceCube point source and a TA UHECR cluster were deemed insignificant due to insufficient statistics. Method: A refined analysis was conducted to test the significance of this potential correlation, utilizing a two-dimensional hypothesis testing approach that incorporates energy resolution for UHECRs and error circles for neutrinos. Result: The study found no statistically significant correlation when evaluating all possible hypotheses. However, a sub-significant correlation was identified for a single specific hypothesis when using a linear significance metric. This sub-signal disappears under a penalty function approach for small-sample size, as well as when considering the relative energy resolution of UHECRs or when one of the flavors is excluded from the IceCube data

By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Our stress data aligns with established models for the slippage and anchored regimes, while we introduce a leverage rule to characterize stresses during stick-slip events. Furthermore, we determine that the transition between stick-slip and anchored regimes is governed by a roughness factor, defined as the ratio of surface asperity size to the radius of curvature of the Plateau borders. This factor effectively captures the explicit dependence of interfacial friction on textured roughness. Additionally, we examine how an increased volume fraction of coarse particles promotes slippage and intensifies stick-slip dynamics. These findings offer crucial insights into the stability of emulsions and foams, which is essential for numerous industrial processes. Additionally, the identified roughness factor may offer a simple metric to assess the anti-icing performance of rough surfaces. When combined with a Bagnold number, this factor helps determine the transition between hysteresis-dominated and roughness-dominated states in drying ice films. Finally, the stick-slip regime is anticipated to be critical for achieving high propulsion speeds in self-propelled droplets on rough boundaries.

We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving multiple primary fingers, toroidal shapes, and mixed configurations. Inextensible membrane simulations reveal the earliest bifurcation forms, which align with a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability, generating sharp spikes on the outer fluid side. Conversely, the expansive nature of the external pressure allows the highly extensible membrane to form a closed droplet shape, resulting in a shape evolution sequence analogous to the classical primary Rayleigh instability of a liquid jet. Furthermore, we introduce a non-dimensional parameter, $\kappa$, that governs the shape of these primary spikes; this parameter can be adjusted to a sufficient degree for the boundary shape to approximate that of a free interface. We also explore the parameter space of wavenumber and growth rate, finding their dependence on system variables to mirror two previously studied cases. Finally, the primary finger solutions generated by an extensible membrane can serve as initial conditions for an inextensible membrane, which can then support multiple primary fingers. # Introduction

Thermodynamics addresses the exchange of energy and matter between a system and its surroundings. While this framework provides invaluable insights and solutions for both equilibrium and many non-equilibrium thermodynamic processes, it relies on macroscopic variables that average over the vast number of microscopic degrees of freedom present in any system. Although the foundational principles of thermodynamics were largely formulated assuming constant system volume, significant applications exist for processes involving volume changes, such as expansion and contraction. Although statistical mechanics offers a pathway to derive non-equilibrium thermodynamics, it presents significant challenges, as the distribution functions of systems driven out of equilibrium often lack analytical even or odd components under time reversal. To overcome these obstacles, we utilize the microcanonical ensemble to examine expansion and contraction. While the number of accessible microstates in the initial and final states differs, we demonstrate that this does not hinder the analysis. We establish a connection between microstates with distinct phase space volumes to explore these processes, subsequently extending the approach to systems subjected to external forces. This extension allows for the determination of non-equilibrium entropy production and confirms that the ensemble average of the product of microstate entropy production and a specific microstate quantity equals its instantaneous value. This link connection method has been employed in prior studies of charge separation and mixing processes. Although we focus on the microcanonical ensemble, the connection principles can be adapted for canonical and grand canonical ensembles to analyze their respective processes.

While numerous prior studies have examined curiosity through self-report methods, they often fail to account for individual differences regarding the intensity, frequency, and temporal variability of curious episodes. This research employs the Experience Sampling Method (ESM) to investigate classroom curiosity across three distinct levels: the moment (e.g., feeling curious for 10 minutes versus 10 hours), the day (e.g., fluctuating intensity on a single day), and the long term. By analyzing data from 101 primary school children sampled 10 times daily for 10 school days, we introduce a novel measurement approach using time-series analysis. This method captures curiosity as a dynamic process characterized by three key metrics: local average intensity, local variability, and local momentum. Through an exploratory analysis, we demonstrate that ESM-measured curiosity is more granular, process-oriented, and distinct from self-report assessments. Despite this prevalence, there is a scarcity of research dedicated to interpreting the internal workings of these scorers. Existing literature suggests that such scorers function as complex "black boxes," a characteristic that fosters an environment susceptible to adversarial attacks. (IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck-Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 1.5 meters in length and having a diameter of 40 centimeters, generates the required plasma environment. Positioned at the source's edge, this plasma region is where both ICRF antenna ports are located. To evaluate the impact of local plasma conditions on antenna performance, a detailed 3D electromagnetic simulation was conducted using the full antenna structure embedded within the source plasma, alongside a detailed 3D plasma geometry. This approach ensures that the antenna's influence on the surrounding plasma is excluded from the analysis. The study examines two distinct plasma length scenarios: a short plasma case (1.0 meter) and a long plasma length case (1.5 meters). Consequently, the antenna is situated at plasma lengths of 0.4 meters relative to the source entrance in the short plasma configuration, and at 1.1 meters relative to the source entrance in the long plasma configuration. The simulation results indicate that when the antenna is coupled to a plasma with a length of 1.0 meters, the plasma acts as an effective low-pass filter for the antenna current, with a cutoff length of 0.96 meters. Conversely, in the 1.5 meter long plasma case, the antenna current exhibits oscillations superimosed on the fundamental frequency, a pattern characteristic of a high-pass filter. These elementary plasma lengths can be effectively achieved on the IShTAR facility. To validate these simulation findings, measurements were performed on a 2-meter long linear plasma using the full antenna assembly. However, the experimental measurements failed to match the simulation outcomes. A critical review of the experimental methodology revealed a significant error in the wave length determination, which was later corrected through a simple post-measurement analysis. Following this correction, the measurements successfully reproduced the antenna current behavior observed in the 1.5 meter long plasma case. Both the simulations and the corrected measurements confirm that an antenna connected to a 1.5 meter long linear plasma acts as a high impedance load, leading to a strong reflection of the forward power. Cancer diagnosis and treatment heavily rely on detecting and counting abnormal cells. We consider a multi-armed bandit framework featuring a contextual side network, where the objective is to maximize the difference between the expected rewards of the selected arm and a specific context. We demonstrate that optimal play reduces to a standard multi-armed bandit problem when a universal constant exists for all arm-reward distributions, as this constant can be disregarded during optimization. When such a constant is absent, we introduce a novel exploration strategy called Exo, designed to exploit relationships within exogenous components. Our empirical tests show that the proposed method can significantly accelerate reinforcement learning.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces significant hurdles when agents interact with non-stationary environments, a problem that intensifies as the count of learning agents rises. This challenge is particularly acute in artificial socialities, a recent paradigm for modeling and constructing complex social systems via interacting MARL agents. To address this, we developed the SocRL library, which offers benchmarks and methods for evaluating MARL agents within artificial socialities, alongside algorithms to mitigate the impact of exogenous states and accelerate training. These methods show strong results on current benchmarks, surpassing existing baselines by up to an order of magnitude, and show promise for applying similar principles to other MARL difficulties.

In recent years, deep learning has rapidly become a primary method for processing data in science and engineering, yet many existing architectures lack a robust theoretical foundation, making models difficult to interpret, validate, or refine using domain knowledge. This work investigates the theoretical underpinnings of widely used Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs). We demonstrate that graph convolutions are equivalent to operations in a graph spectrum, enabling the design of more interpretable and reliable models through standard time-frequency analysis techniques. Accurate mechanical property estimation requires determining tissue displacement, which is typically achieved through cross-correlation techniques. These methods rely on tissue texture, making them susceptible to variations caused by differing anatomical structures. While self-similarity measures have been introduced to supplement correlation, their effectiveness varies across tissue types, potentially yielding inconsistent results. The relationship between these two concepts, as defined by their respective semantic interpretations, remains unclear. This study employs the concept of execution relations from prior research to clarify this dynamic. Specifically, we present the known correspondence between natural deduction and imperative algorithms in new light and demonstrate how this can be extended to sequent calculus. This study extends concepts from computational system design to the construction of recursive functions. We examine the correspondence between natural deduction, including both sequential and recursive forms, and imperative algorithms. A novel contribution of this work is the exploration of the relationship between first-order logic with inductive definitions and nested programs. This correspondence enables the derivation of correct imperative algorithms from natural deduction proofs that do not inherently guarantee correctness. The proposed methods offer a valuable tool for computer scientists, allowing them to learn how to create correct recursive imperative programs even when starting with incorrect attempts. The findings also inform the development of skills for formulating correct recursive algorithms from the outset.

We introduce a method for demonstrating the partial correctness of recursive algorithms based on the interpretation of recursive natural deduction within first-order logic extended with inductive definitions. A key finding of this paper is that this correspondence allows for the generation of algorithms that are not automatically correct. Consequently, the correctness of a specific algorithm must be proven by verifying that its execution relation aligns with the execution of the corresponding recursive proof. This process involves three primary steps: defining the execution relation, establishing a bridge between this relation and imperative syntax, and proving that the relation holds for all relevant inputs. This finding implies that a single natural deduction proof can yield multiple imperative algorithms, with their partial correctness contingent upon the nature of the execution relation. To facilitate this, we provide examples of recursive natural deduction and the associated execution relations, with the last example serving as a case study for creating correct algorithms. We show that two incorrect algorithms can be derived from this specific proof.

The {\em Boolean Ramsey number}, denoted $R(\mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_k)$, is defined as the smallest integer $n$ such that any $k$-coloring of the elements in the Boolean lattice $\mathbf{B}_n$ guarantees the existence of a monochromatic copy of some $\mathbf{P}_i$. This concept was originally introduced by Axenovich, Kaskar, and Schmitt. A pair $(m, n)$ is termed {\em tight} if $R(\mathbf{P}_m, \mathbf{P}_n) = 2^{m+n-1}$. While it is established that $(1, n)$ is tight for all $n$, determining tight pairs with $m, n \geq 1$ remains an open challenge. A recent result by Axenovich and Schmitt shows that if $n \geq 4m$, then $(m, n)$ is also tight. In this paper, we prove that the pair $(m, n)$ is tight for all $n \geq \frac{10m^2}{3} + 4m$. Furthermore, we introduce a new pair of posets, $\langle 2, 2 \rangle$, and demonstrate that $R(\mathbf{B}_2, \mathbf{B}_2) = 11$, thereby establishing that $\langle 2, 2 \rangle$ is a tight pair. \medskip

# Introduction

Contrastive learning has emerged as a powerful technique for leveraging large volumes of unlabeled data, enabling models to capture distinctions between similar and dissimilar inputs. Although recent efforts have successfully employed this method in natural language processing and dialogue systems using relatively small datasets, such models have not yet been thoroughly assessed against real-world data. A recent study even reported that models trained via contrastive learning on the SNORD dataset failed to perform adequately on a 2,000-topic test set derived from Twitter. Although the authors offered simple explanations for this failure, they did not explore alternative strategies to improve model generalization to unseen topics.

We investigate whether incorporating structural information from dialogue graphs during both pre-training and evaluation can help models generalize better to new topics. Our experimental results confirm that learning these structural relationships yields even greater benefits when evaluating on a small number of graphs outside the training set. Furthermore, we demonstrate that effectively integrating graph information does not necessarily require complex architectures; often, just the final layers of an encoder are sufficient to capture necessary structural insights.

At future linear lepton colliders, initial-state radiation (ISR) from leptons is extremely forward-directed, leading to a significant fraction of electrons and positrons exiting the detector's acceptance. This phenomenon causes a sharp decline in collision luminosity at high energies, particularly when a substantial fraction of energy is lost to ISR, as many leptons fail to enter the calorimeters. This issue leads to biased measurements of cross sections for many final states, potentially misinterpreting low-energy tail behavior as a characteristic of new physics rather than an artifact of the measurement. This paper first demonstrates that final states involving hadrons are highly susceptible to these effects, which can be mitigated through lepton tagging or by restricting the photon-energy cut to less than 10%. It then examines states with electron/neutrino or muon/neutrino final states, noting that even with a 50% luminosity reduction, the impact on the electron/neutrino case is severe due to the forward-emitted electron, whereas it can be easily managed in the muon/neutrino scenario via a muon-chamber wheel. Finally, it discusses the benefits of theoretical calculations for these processes, highlighting the need for precise higher-order corrections for future lepton colliders. We conclude that final-state radiation can be handled effectively in most cases, though specific final states require careful attention. These findings underscore the necessity of developing theory calculations capable of final-state hadronization for final states involving hadrons. We also provide links to our public source code. Additionally, we reference previous related work [1] and clarify distinctions from it. If valid, these results mean that many currently available public cross sections may require updates to account for detector effects specific to future TeV-scale lepton colliders. This manuscript introduces a novel algorithm designed to sequentially choose a balanced sample that accommodates both equal and unequal inclusion probabilities. Question sampling, a technique used to gather data from a subset of units within a selected sample, is examined in this manuscript. It is shown that this method can be advantageous in field surveys, particularly when travel costs are involved. The paper presents a new design for sequential question sampling that operates without replacement and does not require the population to be known in advance. This approach is evaluated to determine if it yields more efficient estimates compared to a simple random sample. Additionally, the method's applicability to populations with a known mean is assessed. In all scenarios tested, the findings indicate that the proposed technique performs favorably.

Since numerous image hypotheses often align with both the measurements and prior knowledge, the objective shifts from identifying a single optimal solution to exploring the range of probable hypotheses by sampling the posterior distribution. Images are frequently captured under conditions where portions of the data are missing or corrupted, requiring reconstruction based on strong prior knowledge. In Bayesian imaging, this process involves sampling the posterior distribution to produce numerous realistic hypothesis that fit the measurements. While sampling from complex multimodal distributions is typically a slow operation hindered by complex likelihoods, we show that a conditional generative adversarial network can efficiently generate posterior samples when the data can be transformed into a compact form. We apply this approach to single-coil MRI and inpainting, demonstrating that the resulting hypotheses exhibit Fidelity to Measurements and diversity among their low-frequency components.

Sampling the posterior distribution in inverse problems allows users to explore and evaluate multiple solution hypotheses. While techniques like Markov chain Monte Carlo are well-established, they often fail to capture the full diversity of solutions and suffer from slow convergence, particularly with complex likelihoods. To address this, we propose a conditional generative model that can generate realistic posterior samples at high speed. Our method involves conditioning the generative model on the likelihood and initializing it with the prior distribution. For image superresolution, the model conditions an image given its downsampled version; for single-coil MRI, it conditions an image given multicoil measurements obtained after applying different encoding masks.

In many inverse problem scenarios, the full likelihood function is difficult to evaluate, such as when the data dimension is very high. To overcome this, we develop a method to efficiently compute a close approximation of the likelihood using a conditional autoencoder. This enables the generation of high-fidelity posterior samples with an image-to-image generative adversarial network. Our method

Although high atmospheric absorption typically limits THz links to short ranges, multi-hop directional transmissions can extend coverage. However, traditional beam training methods, including exhaustive searches or fixed-level hierarchical approaches, incur significant time overhead when applied to THz frequencies. To overcome this, the paper introduces a novel adaptive hierarchical beam training scheme that utilizes a feedback channel embedded within the training phase. By reducing the necessary feedback levels in an error-probability-based hierarchical manner, the proposed scheme effectively mitigates the drawbacks of conventional fixed-hierarchy methods. Key parameters, such as the observation window and feedback threshold, are optimized based on local channel state information (CSI) and feedback to optimize system throughput. Simulation results, which account for atmospheric absorption, atmospheric turbulence, and additive white Gaussian noise, demonstrate that the new scheme outperforms conventional hierarchical beam training, particularly in free-space conditions at short distances, by achieving up to 106% higher average system throughput.

This paper presents an analysis of 30 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. Assuming the screens remained relatively stable over this period, we modeled their motion using a quadratic function of time, $at^2+bt+c$, to derive linear velocities and directions from the changes in arc curvature. By combining these velocity data with previously published positional shifts, we calculated the 3D velocities, masses, and locations for all observed arcs and screens. Our results indicate that the two fastest screens behave like a meteoroid—moving rapidly through the solar system and exiting the local interstellar medium—while the two slowest screens share a common kinematic property with the Heliosphere's Vela and Lyra streams, both exhibiting a 45-degree tilt relative to the Local Standard of Rest. These streams are hypothesized to be wakes from a nearby, invisible, high-velocity star. This work further confirms that these streams reside within a conical volume oriented at 30 degrees to the Galactic plane within a 200 pc radius, classifying them as G-type screens. We also report three new screens: a newly discovered solar wind termination shock wave, an older solar system debris object, and a G-type star located 160 pc away. Finally, we propose that all pulsar scintillation screens ultimately originate from one of three categories: (1) solar system debris, (2) meteoroids, or (3) the wakes of high-velocity stars. This suggests that all such screens within a few hundred pc belong to G, K, or M-type stellar streams, or their remnants, lying within the Local Bubble. Since pulsars act as cosmic radar, these findings offer direct evidence against the theory that all stellar winds become turbulent regardless of their host star's type. This conclusion aligns with the observation that the majority of supernovae do not produce stellar wind nebulae. Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, the work cites related research on pulsar wind nebulae, interstellar plasma density, and high-velocity stars. While WN, a causal auto-regressive architecture utilizing dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio generation, its capacity to manage multiple pitches within overlapping dilated receptive fields is insufficient. To resolve this, QPNet employs distinct, tonal convolution kernels tailored to specific pitch ranges, selecting the most appropriate kernel based on the target pitch encoded into the network. Furthermore, to optimize computational efficiency, we implemented kernel pruning and picked units (diluted self-attention) to create a lightweight variant of QPNet. Experiments conducted on the MAESTRO dataset demonstrate that our method effectively generates polyphonic music across various pitches and tempo patterns. The lightweight version achieves comparable performance to the original WN while benefiting from enhanced spectral characteristics. Additionally, mean squared error (MSE) analysis confirms that the light-QPNet matches the output quality of the full QPNet. Finally, listening tests reveal that the light-QPNet surpasses both the original WN and the full QPNet in perceived quality. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ykz242/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. This research was partially supported by JST CREST (JPMJCR2013) and JSPS KAKENHI (JP21H04914).

Despite recent advancements in perceptual quality for generated audio, these systems often demand excessive computational resources, creating a disparity between performance and practical usability. We address this by developing a sparse convolutional neural network framework that maintains perceptual equivalence to a dense baseline while reducing computational cost by an order of magnitude. By leveraging permutations in sparse connectivity, we enable automatic unit-wise pruning and apply this to the densely connected units of a WaveNet. Our method, which incorporates adaptive perceptual loss and sparse connectivity, successfully generates 16kHz-resampled audio with naturalness rivaling the baseline baseline while requiring ten times less computation. This approach is generalizable to other deep generative models with densely connected layers and applies across various sampling rates.

The MADARi framework offers user-friendly interfaces for annotating text and overseeing the annotation workflow, while employing state-of-the-art methods for morphological tagging and spelling to ensure efficient batch processing. This study investigates the atmospheric conditions and resulting emission and transmission spectra for a specific case: an early super-Earth (approximately 2.5 times Earth's mass and 1.3 times Earth's radius) orbiting a K-type star (Teff = 5,300 K) with a semi-major axis (a = 0.08 AU) similar to Mercury's orbital distance. Utilizing the Box-Moondropop model, we simulated the atmospheric evolution, emissions, and transmission spectra of such a planet across various initial volatile inventories and observation times. Our results indicate that a sub-steam atmosphere is unstable, causing any residual volatiles to deplete within 10^6 to 10^7 years. Conversely, if volatiles are present at system formation, the planet retains them; otherwise, it evolves into a bare core within 10^7 years. The generated transmission spectra align well with current detection capabilities, exhibiting distinct water vapor absorption lines at 600-700 nm and 950-1000 nm, as well as a prominent Na I doublet around 590 nm. For emissions, a bare atmosphere yields a spectrum consistent with the continuum, while more complex atmospheric compositions produce spectra with significant line formations. The analysis of this specific planet not only offers valuable insights for upcoming exoplanet observations but also aids in interpreting existing data from the TESS, JWST, and WFC3/IR instruments. This research provides a crucial reference for understanding the formation, evolution, and detection of similar planets in similar systems. In conclusion, if such a planet lost its atmosphere due to stellar radiation, it would become a rocky world devoid of water and an atmosphere, a scenario referred to as the \"Atmosphere Desert\".

This approach involves substituting the standard metallic lead with a resistive lead (large $R$ in k$\Omega$) during tunneling spectroscopy. The significant dissipation effects introduced by the high resistance alter the tunneling conductance in distinct manners. Specifically, the Majorana peak continues to increase as temperature drops, following a power law dependent on $R$, given by $G \propto (\Gamma/R)^{n_M}$ where $\Gamma = e^2/h$ and $n_M = 1/2$ for a canonical Majorana mode. In contrast, a conventional zero-energy peak (associated with a midgap Fermion mode) exhibits a different scaling behavior, $G \propto (\Gamma/R)^{n_F}$, where the exponent $n_F$ varies based on the Fermion mode's conformal dimension. Furthermore, the prefactors in these power-law relationships differ significantly, reflecting the fundamental nature of each mode. This finite-temperature, resistive-tunneling framework provides a more robust characterization of Majorana modes by avoiding uncontrolled proximity-effect heating that can occur in metallic contact configurations. Additionally, it offers a novel perspective on interpreting tunneling experiments utilizing superconducting leads.

Leveraging these capabilities, this paper introduces an automated road inspection system designed to identify and extract FCZs from construction roads. This system employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to process strip images captured by a road inspection vehicle, generating a one-dimensional (1D) mask that delineates the FCZ. The extraction accuracy is assessed using the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC). To ensure reliable and precise extraction, we developed a dual read-write head checkmate (DRW-HCM) network, which consists of a write head network optimized for detection and a read head network optimized for segmentation. During inference, the accuracy of the read head is evaluated against the training set using a sliding window approach to determine the FCZ's boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate that our DRW-HCM network surpasses conventional single-task and multi-task detection and segmentation methods, achieving an extraction AUC of 0.955. Consequently, this system can effectively and automatically delineate FCZs, offering valuable references and insights for road maintenance and risk prevention. In future iterations, we plan to integrate temporal dimension information to further refine extraction accuracy.

Although their graphs often encode rich, high-dimensional data at the node level, GCNs have traditionally relied solely on topological structure because their design is grounded in the homogeneous graph Laplacian. To harness node-attributed information, existing methods like GCNs with attributed structure (GCN-AS) incorporate feature maps and learnable parameters, yet this approach depends heavily on the inherent structure of the input data. This paper introduces the Graph Convolutional Network with Attributed Deformation (GCN-AD), a novel framework that jointly learns with the data's topology and features. By applying a deformation function to the original graph, GCN-AD maps nodes with similar high-dimensional features to neighboring nodes, thereby simultaneously preserving both topological and feature information. The main contributions are: (1) the application of a deformation function to attract nodes with similar features, creating an enhanced data structure; and (2) the use of this enhanced structure as input to a GCN for classification. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate that GCN-AD outperforms various state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, an ablation study on a disease classification dataset reveals that the proposed deformation function effectively enhances data structures. Consequently, GCN-AD serves as a powerful tool for joint learning of topological and feature information, with potential applications in data clustering, ranking, and other areas. The code will be available at https://github.com/zhengyuan0825/GCN-AD.

Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have recently achieved significant success in tasks such as data clustering, ranking, and segmentation. This performance gain is largely attributed to the incorporation of graph information, and recent advancements have even enabled knowledge sharing among graphs. However, most current methods are restricted by the limitations of the data's original structure. To address this, we integrate a graph optimization function into the message passing framework of GCNs, allowing the graph to be jointly learned with the features. This approach is broadly applicable to any data that can be represented as a graph. Theoretically, the approach is sound because the learned representation should inherently capture both topological and feature information. Empirically, an improved graph directly leads to better classification accuracy. We present an analysis of the method's limitations, discuss related work, and provide a comparison with other techniques. For this system, we establish uniqueness and derive stability estimates for the source term using a single boundary measurement of the "structure." The uniqueness proof relies on Carleman estimates, while the stability result is achieved through an observability inequality combined with a compactness/uniqueness argument. Finally, an operator theoretic approach provides the necessary regularity for the initial conditions to attain the desired stability estimate. A byproduct of this work is a new, simplified proof of global uniqueness and stability (both T- and H^1-type) for a boundary coefficient in a structural acoustic system devoid of a source term. This system features a Laplacian, a first-order time derivative, and fourth-order Laplacian terms with distinct positive coefficients; the boundary term couples the limits of these three operators. Notably, the structural acoustic model represents the simplest system exhibiting third-order parabolic behavior. The primary application of this finding is to leverage standard unique continuation properties of elliptic operators, such as the Laplacian, for the structural acoustic PDE model. The main innovation of the paper lies in a novel "regularity by stability" framework, which provides a direct path to stability and regularity estimates for a broad class of partial differential equation systems, encompassing many cases where existing methods are inapplicable. In this scenario, acoustic pressure satisfies the Helmholtz equation, while the boundary condition on the obstacle involves the acoustic admittance, defined as the ratio of normal acoustic velocity to normal acoustic acceleration. The primary contribution of the paper is formulating the scattering problem as an equivalent source problem (ESP) valid throughout the exterior domain, encompassing the immediate vicinity of the obstacle. Specifically, the actual field generated by a source in the entire exterior domain (including the neighborhood of the obstacle) is equivalent to that produced by an ESP located strictly on the obstacle's surface. Notably, the ESP resides on the boundary, whereas the problem under consideration is defined on the external domain excluding the obstacle. The ESP comprises a combination of monopoles, dipoles, and quadrapoles. While the Helmholtz equationgoverns the ESP in the external domain, the specific distribution of these components on the obstacle surface yields the total acoustic field, matching the original field exactly at the boundary. To validate the proposed approach, we employ the ESP alongside the Boundary Element Method (BEM) for the Helmholtz equation, demonstrating results across a range of frequencies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ESP distribution exhibits singular behavior as the frequency approaches zero, with the strength of these singularities increasing near corners and edges of the obstacle. Finally, the feasibility of solving the ESP using BEM is discussed.
